title: Taste at scale
description: The agency model was always a headcount problem. More clients meant more people. Margins stayed thin because the work couldn’t scale faster than the team. Every studio I watched operate ran into the same ceiling: the work was good, the growth was slow, and the business was fragile. I built Nirmata to see whether one person with the right tools and judgment could do what used to require a team of eight. The answer is yes. With a few things worth saying out loud. The economics changed Software used to be expensive to build . Three things collapsed at roughly the same time: the cost of execution, the cost of coordination, and the cost of custom software. When those three things were expensive, you needed specialists for each, and a project manager to stitch them together. When they got cheap, the specialists became overhead. AI writing code is the obvious story. The less obvious one is what that does to project economics. . A custom interface that used to require two weeks of a senior developer’s time can come together in days. A design system that would have needed a dedicated sprint now gets built alongside the thing it governs. The friction between design and development, the handoff cost that every agency has tried and failed to eliminate, shrinks to almost nothing when one person is handling both ends with AI in the loop. That’s the mechanical case for Nirmata. Design and development as a single continuous process, owned by one studio, delivered at a pace the traditional model structurally can’t match. Where product work actually breaks Most product work fails at the boundary between disciplines. The designer doesn’t understand what’s expensive to build. The developer doesn’t know which edge cases the design was trying to solve. The PM is translating between them and losing signal in both directions. By the time something ships, it’s a negotiated object, shaped more by coordination cost than by the original intent. Whoever can hold design, engineering, and product decisions in the same head and act on all three without waiting for a meeting will outshine a committee every time. What gets cheaper is execution. What stays expensive is knowing what to build, why it matters, and whether the thing you shipped is actually working. Coding agents accelerate shipping, which puts pressure on the part that teams have always struggled with most. That part has stayed stubbornly manual, even as everything around it gets automated. A ticket manager who creates tasks and tracks status is overhead in this model. Judgment isn’t. A studio that controls the full cycle removes most of the translation steps. The thinking that shapes the design is the same thinking that decides how it gets built. That continuity shows up in the work. What the freed space is for The design founder era is partly about aesthetics and partly about this. Founders who can hold the visual and the technical in the same head reliably build things that feel coherent. The interface and the system underneath it are solving the same problem, in the same register. When agents handle the implementation, something shifts. The cognitive overhead of writing code drops out, and the mental space it occupied goes somewhere else. For me, it goes toward the psychology of what gets built. Why does this pattern create anxiety? Why does this flow cause people to abandon? What does this decision cost the user versus what it earns the product? I’ve spent years building a library of over a hundred psychological principles that apply directly to product decisions, documented at 1984.design . Loss aversion, cognitive load, the peak-end rule, decision fatigue. Applied directly, they separate a feature that serves users from one that extracts from them. Dark patterns (aka deceptive patterns ) exist because most builders never slow down enough to ask whether what they’re shipping is actually good for the person on the other end. Coding with agents creates that space. The speed is a side effect. The more important thing is what you can think about while the code gets written. The caution YC’s Spring 2026 request list named it: AI-native agencies running at software-level margins, same output, none of the coordination cost. A model that treats headcount as a variable, not a fixed input. Nirmata was built on that assumption before the framing existed. AI-written code still needs someone accountable for what it does. Security, reliability, IP, those don’t disappear because the code came fast. I treat oversight as part of the work, not something you add at the end. What remains AI absorbed the execution layer. What’s left is editorial work: knowing what to build, recognizing when it’s right, deciding when to stop. The design bar will keep rising alongside this. Builders who ship more can iterate faster, which means the gap between good taste and no taste compounds over time. AI also improves its own design output , so even companies for whom design wasn’t a priority will get access to better defaults. The premium moves entirely to taste, the ability to recognize what works, what doesn’t, and why. A one-person studio doing the full cycle lives in that space. Which problems are worth solving. Which tradeoffs to accept. How to hold a coherent vision from the first conversation to the thing that ships. AI handles the rest. That’s why I’m building Nirmata . Thanks for reading. — B.

title: #307 | Cronicamente offline
description: nas edições anteriores #305 | Offline é o novo hype (parte 2) #306 | Uma seleção de campanhas tempo de leitura: 5 minutos para entender 💡 “A habilidade mais importante do próximo século não vai ser conectar humanos com mais tecnologia. Vai ser conectar humanos uns com os outros”. _ “Ninguém confia no gosto de quem só consome fast-food”. _ Em 2025, a WGSN já tinha previsto que a fadiga digital e o excesso de estímulos levaria as pessoas a migrarem para comunidades no mundo real: “Até 2027, a busca por menos barulho e mais desconexão digital vai ser o novo normal, emergindo como uma demonstração de autocuidado em forma de ambientes mais calmos, seguros e significativos” Isso tem se traduzido na realização e/ou incentivo de todo tipo de experiência. Um grande destaque no Brasil, que ilustra tanto o pertencimento quanto o autocuidado e, claro, a presença das marcas, são as corridas de rua. Segundo a Exame , em 2024 foram realizadas 2.827 corridas de rua oficiais no país. Em 2025, mais de 5 mil. Além disso, temos visto o crescimento de eventos em lojas, jantares especiais para clientes, clubes do livro, exibições em salas de cinema e convites para as mais diversas atividades físicas, manuais, intelectuais e sociais. E assim seguirá essa tendência - em 2027 e além. O que nos traz à edição de hoje é a sua relação com a creator economy . No que o Digiday chamou de “ vibes over metrics ”, os eventos presenciais agora são também uma estratégia de engajamento e construção de comunidade para marcas pessoais - ou marcas essencialmente virtuais. _ Três movimentos estão por trás disso: 1 - O mundo “pós-feed”, em que as redes sociais se tornaram oficialmente plataformas de descoberta e entretenimento, e onde “número de seguidores” é uma métrica cada vez menos determinante de sucesso e engajamento. Hoje, a viralização está muito mais ligada à adequação de um conteúdo a um nicho, assunto, tom ou formato (ou todos ao mesmo tempo). Mas quando encontrar uma audiência tem se tornado mais fácil, aprofundar essa relação é o desafio. Seja criando um universo de marca que gere reconhecimento e lembrança, seja reunindo essas pessoas para além do feed. 2 - A busca por mais presença , que é comum a todas as gerações e todos os nichos - todo mundo gostaria de ter mais atenção, mais concentração e mais serendipidade na vida. O que varia muito é como isso acontece. Quais rituais alguém pode incorporar ao seu dia a dia? Qual a periodicidade ideal desses encontros? Qual a atmosfera perfeita para proporcionar aquilo que alguém mais precisa? Assim como fazem com o seu conteúdo, seja lifestyle, seja desenvolvimento profissional, a curadoria e capacidade de simplificar informações dos creators tem muito valor aqui. O que nos traz ao próximo ponto. 3 - O tal do repertório, que nunca se falou tanto em construir, mas que não está nos mesmos vídeos ou carrosseis virais que todo mundo está compartilhando. Repertório é o que se traduz em uma perspectiva única que só aquela pessoa consegue trazer, com base em tudo que ela carrega consigo. Textos, imagens, experiências, tudo aquilo que você já viu e vivenciou, o lugar da onde você vem, os lugares por onde já passou, as boas conversas, os livros fáceis ou difíceis, os hábitos diários e ambientes que frequenta… Tudo isso forma o seu repertório. Que pode ser composto, sim, pelo que passa pelo feed e vai morar na sua pasta de “salvos” ou no mosaico mental de referências que você acessa a cada job. Mas um ponto de vista realmente original não vem de consumir mais do mesmo, ou apenas o que é filtrado por algoritmos. Vem de uma vida interessante o suficiente para influenciar tudo que você faz. Uma vida que acontece através de telas, mas principalmente fora delas. Naqueles ambientes em que conseguimos estar presentes com todo o nosso corpo (não apenas os nossos dedos em contato com uma tela fria). Naqueles momentos em que uma informação é registrada não porque é vista, mas porque é vivida, com todas as nuances do ambiente, das pessoas que estão ali e de como ela é apresentada. No conhecimento que alguém realmente tem para passar - sem ferramentas que escrevem roteiros, sem a chance de regravar até ficar bom o suficiente. Nas trocas que a gente não consegue pensar antes de digitar ou gravar duas ou três vezes antes de enviar. Depois de anos cronicamente online, é por essas e outras que o conteúdo, a influência e as comunidades têm buscado o offline. _ Quando “comunidade” era a grande tendência nos relatórios, a gente se tornava uma. Quando carrosséis anunciavam o retorno das revistas impressas, a nossa já estava na gráfica. Quando certos produtos físicos estavam virando colecionáveis, o nosso boné esgotou em 24 horas. Agora, chegou a vez da gente olhar para o offline - como movimento de mercado e necessidade humana - do único jeito que a gente sabe fazer: ✨ na prática ✨ Topam ser uma comunidade presencial também? :) Nosso encontro está marcado no dia 27 de outubro, terça-feira, na Avenida Paulista. Com direito a revista impressa e convidados mais que especiais. As vagas são limitadas, e o cupom NEWSLETTER dá 15% de desconto para as dez primeiras pessoas vindas aqui da news: vem para o Bits Ao Vivo para inspirar ✨ A marca americana Altra Running anunciou o seu Altra Legacy Team - a equipe de corrida mais velha do mundo. Imprevisível pelas pesquisas, ele demonstrou o retorno do fenômeno “22 confirma”, que elegeu candidatos de postura e currículo extremamente questionáveis sob o guarda-chuva do bolsonarismo. title: The two forces that help build opportunity
description: Hey pals, I hope all is good in your world. Today we are going to dive a little deeper into two very important elements that build recognisable reputations and brands… and why I built the Opportunity Design Course + Course Club (Early Bird enrollment closes this Sunday!). The two elements? Perception & Evidence. Firstly I want to explain what these two things are individually. Evidence: This is what you’ve actually done. It’s the real, tangible proof of your work. The products you’ve built, the testimonials you’ve earned from your clients, the projects you’ve delivered to your people, the impact you’ve created as a whole. It’s the truth, the receipts, the stuff that stands up in a court of freaking law. Perception: This is what people think you’ve done. It’s how your brand is experienced from the outside. It’s the story that forms in someone’s head long before they ever meet you, talk to you, or work with you. Simply put... Evidence = what is true and provable. Perception = what people believe to be true based on what they can see. The big old problem we all have as creative humans, especially those who have been in the game for a fair chunk of time... it’s impossible for anyone to have access to ALL of your evidence. Most people won’t see the hours you’ve poured in a project, the thinking behind your decisions, or how much bloody effort goes into what you do every damn day. They often just see the end result and that’s where their opinion forms. That’s why perception, in many cases, outweighs evidence... and why perception is super important in brand building. You could be absolutely brilliant at what you do, but if nobody knows it, it doesn’t exist in their world. You might have the work to back it up, but if the way you show up looks sloppy or inconsistent... or you do not show up at all... people will think twice and find another option. That doesn’t mean perception is about pretending or faking it for the internet or your clients in general. It’s about making it easier for people to find the truth, and to do that, you need to give them access to your evidence. Our job as humans who own businesses is to make sure the perception of us from the outside aligns with the truth as closely as possible. Trust doesn’t come from either perception or evidence on its own… it grows when the two work together, and as you can see from the image below, that’s when you become a Power Brand. I personally believe we are all striving to become the “Power Brand” where our perception and evidence are high and in alignment, and the gap between them is very small. This is where true value is created and we become a much safer commercial choice for our clients. Opportunity happens consistently when the truth and perceived reality are best mates, standing together. Here is a little breakdown of each quadrant so you can understand where you might sit. High perception, high evidence: The Power Brand. People notice you and consistently experience the quality behind the perception. Your reputation matches the reality of what you actually deliver, which creates trust, momentum, and long-term opportunity. Every great brand we know masters this balance between perception and evidence. High perception, low evidence: The Hype Brand. You know how to grab attention and create excitement, but the reality underneath hasn’t fully caught up yet. Things can look bigger, stronger, or more established from the outside than they actually are once people get closer. Low perception, high evidence: The Hidden Genius Brand. You’re doing brilliant work, but not enough people currently get the chance to experience it. The skill, care, and trustworthiness are already there… your reputation just hasn’t spread far beyond your existing network yet. (I built Opportunity Design for you my friends) Low perception, low evidence: The Work-in-Progress Brand. You’re still figuring things out, experimenting, learning, and discovering where your strengths actually live. And honestly? That’s completely normal. Every powerful brand, business, and creative human starts as a work in progress. The big takeaway here? Branding isn’t just about reality... it’s also about perceived reality. People can’t choose you based on the evidence they have never seen. They can only choose you based on what they know, and ultimately, believe to be true about you. This is why I am so excited about The Opportunity Design Course + Course Club that starts next week. This is a 6-week programme designed to help you close the gap between what you’re capable of and what other people know you’re capable of, in order to create more extraordinary opportunities. I designed this for the Hidden Geniuses who need their perception to catch up with their evidence on their way to becoming a Power Brand. Join before 11:59pm Pacific Time Sunday, 11th October to grab a bonus 1:1 call with me and save $150 off the regular price. Inside the course, I share with you how I have intentionally created opportunities over the last few years with a super simple (but takes effort) system for building your perception up to align with all your existing evidence. I will show you how to prove you are valuable to the right people before they see value in you themselves. I will show you my frameworks to build commercial relationships that increase the probability of you being chosen. Here’s everything included: 12 pre-recorded lessons covering the Opportunity Design system. Six weeks of live group coaching, with a 90-minute call each week on Wednesdays. Our first call is Wednesday, 14th October. A private community space to stay connected, share what you’re learning, ask questions, and cheer each other on. Weekly action tasks to help you turn the lessons into progress. A 90-day Perception Reset Plan to follow after the course. That call is time to focus on your situation and the work you want, the people you want to reach, and how you can help them see more of what you’re capable of. If you’ve ever wanted to chat with me 1:1, this is your chance my friends. The programme starts with live calls every Wednesday starting on the 14th October . Join before 11th October to get the discount and your one-to-one call. JOIN THE OPPORTUNITY DESIGN COURSE CLUB No hacks, no shortcuts my friends. This is a creative way to become recognised as a human with a creative brain, and work on becoming a Power Brand. Let’s freaking go. James The People’s Branding Mentor Questions? description: nas edições anteriores #300 | A vida das coisas #301 | O legado da Copa do Mundo 2026 tempo de leitura: 4 minutos para entender 💡 do dicionário: oráculo, substantivo masculino Num lugar sagrado, resposta a uma pergunta feita a uma divindade cujo teor era entendido como profético, sendo de difícil compreensão, obscuro. Resposta dada por uma divindade, quando alguém a consultava. Pessoa que, supostamente, prevê o futuro ou a previsão feita por essa pessoa. _ Nada contra carrosseis de Instagram. Inclusive, fazemos vários. O formato inicialmente permitia compartilhar dez imagens em um único post, e depois foi expandido para vinte. Primeiro, foi utilizado pelos millennials como álbum do Orkut - registros agrupados de um mesmo evento. Depois a gen Z, querendo performar menos, intercalou fotos posadas com fotos aleatórias e chamou de dump . Enquanto isso, a bolha criadora de conteúdo tratava as telas como slides e elaborava apresentações sobre todo tipo de assunto - com call to action no final, claro. Salve, compartilhe, assine, contrate, inscreva-se. O carrossel é um dos formatos preferidos de quem busca engajamento. Basta um questionamento bem amplo e chamativo na capa, seguido por uma série de telas que ora explicam, ora confundem. O resultado é a banalização de questões extremamente profundas - como se a resposta coubesse em um carrossel de Instagram. Ou como se eles fossem de fato lidos com a devida atenção, ou escritos com a pretensão de elaborar uma pauta para além do rage bait da capa. Como se eles fossem sequer escritos por uma outra pessoa. _ Nada contra carrosseis de Instagram. Inclusive, fazemos vários. É muito útil poder intercalar explicações com imagens, organizar textos de forma compartilhável, ampliar discussões e aumentar a audiência sem depender de vídeos curtos. A inteligência artificial é uma grande aliada nesta organização de informações e layout para expressar ideias. Agora, a disseminação dos carrosseis feitos por inteligência artificial, posicionando suas fontes como oráculos contemporâneos das gerações, do brasileiro ou de qualquer tipo de comportamento tem servido mais para vender, do que para informar. No grande mercado que virou a timeline, a atual recomendação é juntar o questionamento profundo com a elaboração rasa e o call to action certo no final. Assim, vamos arrastando para cima de uma pergunta para outra e delegando a nossa capacidade de reflexão ao marketing digital. De repente, parece que questões complexas cabem nesse tipo de generalização, que gerações inteiras podem ser reduzidas a frases de efeito, ou que estratégias elaboradas podem ser decifradas em algumas telas. _ Perguntas são feitas desde que o mundo é mundo. A busca por respostas, inclusive, talvez seja mais importante na nossa evolução do que o momento em que elas são encontradas. Seguir sem respostas talvez seja uma das coisas mais inspiradoras que existem. O que muda é o contexto em que perguntas surgem e respostas são elaboradas. title: The Industry Swap Experiment
description: An amazingly random thing happened this last week. I found myself in Moab, Utah, with around 70 total strangers who now feel like my best friends. I was invited by my buddy Jason to speak at the first-ever Summer Camp hosted by his company, Rupt, for the promotional products industry. There were team colours, a healthy dose of friendly competition, prizes, adventures and learning sessions, all set against the incredible backdrop of the Colorado River and the red rock desert. It was fucking Magical. As a brand guy I often find myself around brand people whether thats agency owners, designers or people building things in the creative space but I have always loved to pop myself in the deep water of the unknowing. I know very little about this world. Like most people, I’ve interacted with the industry countless times as an end user. Whether that’s branded merch, company swag, event giveaways or promotional products arriving in the post… but I’ve never actually spent too much time inside the industry itself or with the people who make it all happen… so on paper, I had absolutely no business being there. But that’s exactly why I jumped at the chance to speak at this event. I love learning new things, and this room was packed with some of the biggest hitters in the game. People who have spent years building businesses and solving problems in a world I know jack shit about. It would have been easy to say no. The travel was long, the industry was unfamiliar but saying no to this opportunity was never really on the cards for me. I am getting older, and as that happens, the more I think one of the biggest mistakes we make is only learning from people who do the same thing as us. We all read the same design books, follow pretty much the same people, attend the same conferences and end up having the same conversations over and over again. This felt like the exact opposite of that… I’m gonna call it the ‘anti-echo chamber’ move. An opportunity to step outside my own little corner of the world and spend time with people who think differently and see things through a completely different lens. I had a feeling it would open my brain up in ways it hadn’t been before, and it absolutely did. Now, even though this space doesn’t live and breathe design in the same way mine does, it still lives in the world of branding. Most brand people spend their time on the fun stuff like the thinking, story, and execution side of design. We help make strategic decisions, build the identity, and create the funky punky assets. Then, more often than not, we release the work into the wild and hope it finds its way. What really hit home for me whilst spending time with this incredible group of humans is that this industry is actually much closer to mine than I first realised. They’re positioned at an incredibly important point in the journey… where the identity of a company meets real humans in the real world. They are a key part of what we do because they help bring businesses to life through experiences. And ultimately, that’s where ‘brand status’ is earned. As brand people, we’re in the game of pattern building and memory. We help businesses become recognisable. The promotional products industry helps those companies show up in the real world, creating physical touch-points and experiences that reinforce everything the business is trying to stand for. The biggest takeaway for me this week, apart from the fact that Moab might be one of the coolest places on the planet, is that every industry has its own wisdom. Every industry has people solving interesting problems and has a lot of knowledge to offer the general outsider who is keen to learn a new perspective. It’s easy to convince ourselves that all the answers live inside our own little bubble, but I’ve found over the years that many of the best ideas and implementations in my own business have come from looking outside of design. Whether that’s borrowing hospitality thinking and applying it to my design process, or building an identity of my own that fuses tattoo culture with skate-shop vibes, the things that have helped me stand out have not come from simply doing what everyone else was doing. One of the ideas I shared during my talk was Hotelling’s Law … the observation that competitors naturally drift towards sameness because it feels safer. Over time, everyone starts looking similar, sounding similar and offering similar things because nobody wants to stray too far from what appears to be working for others. The irony though is that the safest thing to do often becomes the riskiest thing to do. If everybody moves towards the middle, the middle becomes really freaking crowded. Which is why I’ve always been more interested in pushing at the edges… That’s where the interesting opportunities live. That’s why I think we should all spend a little more time making anti-echo chamber moves. Here are some ways you can do that: 1. Go to the event that isn’t built for you. 2. Read the book that nobody in your industry is talking about. 3. Spend time with people who challenge your assumptions. 4. Put yourself in rooms where you’re not the expert. Remember, my friends… curiosity is often where the magic lives. And if my week in the Utah desert taught me anything, it’s that sometimes the most valuable thing you can do isn’t go deeper into your own world… It’s to spend some time exploring somebody else’s. Big love and respect. James - The People’s Branding Mentor

title: Tiny moments that become a real brand.
description: Before we jump into this week’s article, reminder that my new book No Bullsh*t Branding is available for pre-order… and if you pre-order by the end of today (Sunday 31st May) you get a bonus freebie bundle, including the Book Club, the new MVB Course, limited edition MBJ merch, and digital downloads. Check it out here ! Thank you all so much for your support. Last weekend the weather was delicious. So delicious that myself, Kate and Rocco went to the beach for the day to hang with our friends (Jamie & Mel) and their little kiddos… it was one of those beautiful little days that will live long in the memory bank. We were down at West Wittering beach near Chichester. It’s this big, magical stretch of sand where, when the tide goes out, the beach becomes absolutely colossal. Perfect for kids because there’s endless space to run around and play… it becomes the worlds largest, sandy adventure space. Scattered across the beach are these little pools of warm water left behind by the retreating tide… tiny, stinky lakes full of seaweed, shells, wet sand and mess. Basically heaven for a little dude like Rocco. And he was more than happy exploring them completely alone while the rest of his friends sat further up the beach eating lunch and digging holes. He was so happy, so I wanted him to just ‘be’… so I stayed and watched. After maybe an hour of watching him play in the same giant puddle, I eventually wandered up to him and asked him to come back to “base camp” so we could put more suncream on, tag mummy back in and potentially allow me to eat some lunch. But he was having absolutely none of it. Everything I offered was ignored. Every negotiation tactic I’d learned in business was useless, and every attempt to reason with him about how the sun was really hot and he needed protecting from it was completely pointless. Eventually Kate, my wonderful wife, spotted my slow descent into parental defeat from afar and wandered over with all the supplies we needed. And at that point, I just accepted reality and decided to play the waiting game until he was ready to move on himself… I mean, the sun would go down eventually, I was sure of that, and I also now had a sandwich. But there was a lesson hiding inside all of this. When you have very little to negotiate with, the situation you are in becomes incredibly difficult to win… and this got me thinking about the very beginning of my own business journey. It was so difficult to find any money-making opportunities when I started because I had so little to negotiate with. No Leverage. I had no real portfolio, no website, no testimonials and, in absolute honesty… very little knowledge. I wouldn’t have hired me. As you know, for me, a brand is a recognisable reputation, and at that point I was neither recognised nor did I really have a reputation worth knowing… unless it was “having a good time down the pub” - I was real good at that. And this got me thinking about all the newbies entering the world right now. All the junior creatives trying to find work and carve out a place for themselves while also navigating challenges I never had to deal with. Things like social media pressure, constant comparison, AI, tech and the heavy, heavy, heavy psychological weight of feeling like you need to live your life so publicly online. Now, I’m not saying my era had it easy at all… every generation has its own struggles. But I do think it’s harder now than it was 20 years ago, mainly for the reasons I mentioned above. So I want to try an answer this question today. How do we build a business when, right at the beginning, we have nothing to be recognised for and no reputation backing us up? So… lets chat. Yes, you might not have the clients yet. You might not have the case studies, the swanky portfolio, the testimonials or the years of industry proof backing up your ambition. But what you do have is YOU. That matters far more than many people think. Because there are already so many things you are recognised for outside of your “business circles”. Your attitude, your energy, your humour, your kindness, your curiosity, your willingness to help, your ability to make people feel good around you, your ability to stay optimistic when everything feels difficult or half empty. What I’m trying to suggest here is that even if you do not yet have a recognisable reputation around your work, you already have years and years of building a recognisable reputation around your humanness and character, and that is a beautifully fun place to start… that becomes your negotiating power. One of the huge advantages early stage creatives have is that they are not yet boxed in by the “rules” of the industry. They are not trapped by client expectations or weighed down by years of process refinement and predictability. They still have “all the raws”… raw energy, raw enthusiasm and raw creativity to boot. In the beginning, it’s often your willingness to care about others and build relationships that sparks the most opportunity. Helping a mate out for freebies, offering your services to friends of friends in exchange for tickets to their latest gig… that scrappy little world of free crafty goodness is where most of us cut our teeth in the industry. When I was starting out, I bartered constantly. I used my skills to build experience, and the more experience I gained, the more confidence I built. In return, I’d get free coffee, free jewellery, free food, whilst also building relationships with local humans… whatever people could offer at the time instead of money, I said yes to. Looking back, I actually think there’s something incredibly beautiful about that stage of the journey. I mean, bartering is how worlds were built. When you’re starting out, you still have permission to try almost anything you can to keep the lights on and keep the dream alive. You can knock on doors, start conversations, help people, make things, experiment, build fabulous little ditties and push your creativity out into the world. And over time, people begin recognising you for those behaviours. For your energy, your effort, your generosity, your consistency and the way you make people feel. Almost without noticing it, those tiny moments become the foundations of a recognisable reputation. A real brand. So if you are at the beginning, listening to a noisy world telling you that “designers are fucked” or “the creative industry is doomed,” remember that most of it is just distraction… like a lot of news on the inter webs. Don’t fall into the trap of blindly listening to these people. Many of them have their own agenda too… which is often making sure they stay relevant and irreplaceable in a changing world. Instead, use your creativity and your energy to build relationships. Make cool stuff and send it to people. Write a little hand-drawn note thanking somebody for inspiring you. Instead of sending the same PDF portfolio to 400 people like everybody else is doing, start more real, human conversations. Barter your services. Collaborate with people. Send a hand written letter. Deliver someone a little product with your work on it. Go above and beyond simply because you care enough to do so. Become recognised for how much effort you are putting in… that is a reputation that opportunities will eventually flow towards. Stay Focused, Stay Crafty… Your creativity is your super duper power. James - The Peoples Branding Mentor

title: The Unscriptable Moments That Build Reputation
description: Hello my champions of creative goodness. How are ya? Today I want to dive into a little topic that I am super passionate about, and that is the human goodness we can do to elevate the experience for the people we work with. Everyone reading this is a craft-based, creativity-infused builder of things. You might own a business, work with brands, or create cool visuals for people who love looking at cool visuals. I don’t think creative people like that need motivation to continue doing the things they already do so well, but I do think there is another layer we often forget to think about… the human layer. The stuff on top of the craft. That is where some new magic can be found. It looks like over the coming years a lot of businesses and brands will automate huge parts of their customer journey, which is logical, so the question for me becomes… Where does the human come in and make a decision that was not obvious? I am all for becoming more efficient and dialling in a good process, as many of you will know, but it’s often the stupid-on-paper, “not good for business” decisions that build a reputation worth talking about. One of my favourite examples of human creativity elevating a brand’s reputation is the story of Joshie the Giraffe. A family went on holiday to California and accidentally left their son’s stuffed giraffe at a Ritz-Carlton hotel where they were staying. To put the little boy at ease, his dad told a little white lie and said Joshie had decided to stay behind for an extra holiday. The dad had phoned the hotel and asked if they could find it, send it back, and hopefully reunite the little guy with his giraffe. The hotel staff found Joshie amongst the laundry and could have simply posted the toy back. But instead, they created an entire photo album showing Joshie relaxing by the pool, driving golf carts, getting spa treatments with cucumbers over his eyes, and “enjoying his extended vacation” before finally sending him home, all to back up his dad’s story. That tiny, unscriptable moment of human creativity transformed a forgotten toy into a story that millions of people still talk about today… just like I am right now. And I think that’s freaking fascinating. Because I doubt that family remembers much about the facilities at the Ritz-Carlton, the weather, or even how good the food was… but they will absolutely remember Joshie’s holiday forever. This got the old curiosity up… Why do moments like this stick with us so deeply while so many other experiences disappear from memory almost immediately? Why do we instantly want to tell our mates about them, repost them online and emotionally connect with complete strangers because of them? For that we probably need to get a little ‘sciencey’. Now remember, I’m not a scientist. I’m just an inquisitive bloke with a scraggly beard who spends far too much time researching human behaviour, but here’s what I found out… Your brain is basically a very clever prediction machine. Most of the time, your brain is trying to conserve energy by guessing what is about to happen next based on previous experiences and familiar patterns. If things go exactly as expected, the brain doesn’t need to pay much attention because nothing new or important is happening. Win for brain power. This is why most of our routine experiences disappear from memory almost immediately. If you are anything like me, you get in the car, drive somewhere you’ve been a thousand times before, pull up, get out, and suddenly realise you barely even remember the journey itself. You obviously drove, stopped at traffic lights and avoided crashing into things, but because your brain already knew the pattern, most of the drive happened on complete autopilot… and it’s even easier now I don’t have to change gears anymore. Thank fook for the automatic. Humans do this constantly. We predict things, filter things and automate familiar experiences because if we had to consciously process every tiny detail of every moment of every day we would mentally collapse before our cheeky 11am coffee break. That’s why so many experiences we go through every single day become, well… forgettable. You expect the hotel room to be ready when you arrive. You expect somebody at reception to hand you a key, point you towards the lift or stairs and solve any mini problems in the quickest and most logical way possible, so when all of those things happen exactly as predicted, your brain simply processes the experience efficiently and moves on because nothing emotionally interesting actually happened. But when something interrupts that predictable pattern in a creative, emotional or unexpected way, your brain suddenly pays far more attention because it wasn’t expecting it. That’s why the Joshie story mattered so freaking much. The family expected the hotel to find the giraffe and simply post it back. Problem solved. No dramas here people. Everybody moves on with their lives. But instead, the hotel staff created this ridiculously brilliant, fake holiday for the giraffe that made it feel like Joshie was genuinely out there living his best life in the California sun and making mates along the way. They went to completely unreasonable measures just to bring a little bit of joy to a child and back up his dad’s white lie, and that exact unpredictability is what made the whole thing unforgettable. Humans remember meaningful and surprising moments far more than they remember predictable and functional ones. The hotel didn’t just solve the problem. They transformed a completely ordinary customer service interaction into a story that people are still retelling years later… and I think that’s the bit most of us miss as business owners. People rarely remember what was efficient, but they almost always remember how something made them feel. I mean, I almost bloody cried the first time I read the Joshie story because I instantly thought about how my own son would feel seeing his favourite toy off living its best life and making mates on holiday. I take Lightning McQueen with me on work trips because I miss my son Rocco, and I take silly little photos of him at random places because I know my son lights up when he sees them. He genuinely thinks daddy and Lightning are away together having a good time, so this little giraffe story hit a proper emotional note for me. The Joshie story stopped being “good customer service” and instantly became something far more human because you could feel the love, effort and humanity inside the decision those hotel staff made… and that kind of creativity can never be automated. Nor bloody should it. I hope this story sparks the creativity inside you to go against the grain when you can. To be unpredictable with your kindness and to find ways to connect with others that might be out of the ordinary. People remember people who thought about them in different and unique ways. I think, over the coming years, businesses and brands will increasingly be judged on what they choose to keep human. Automate the predictable. Humanise the meaningful. Love ya. James - The People’s Branding Mentor

title: Tesla launches flying Roadster concept car
description: Electric car company Tesla has unveiled its flying Roadster vehicle with a demonstration in which the car drove upside down, flipped off a ramp and briefly flew, using compressed-air thrusters that Tesla claims will make it the world's quickest production car. During a live event in Texas, the two-seat Roadster model drove up a half-pipe ramp and launched off the top, remaining in the air for a few seconds before landing It also became airborne after building up speed on flat ground, launching over a row of parked vehicles. It then lifted off from a stationary position. Tesla has unveiled its second-generation Roadster A series of thrusters in the bottom and back propelled the car into the air and cushioned the landings. It was designed by Tesla and SpaceX, both companies led by businessman Elon Musk, who called the second-generation Roadster "a collaboration with the world's best car company and the world's best rocket company". It has thrusters that use compressed air The thrusters can also fire rearward to boost acceleration. Tesla demonstrated the car reaching 60 miles per hour in a claimed 0.81 seconds, and said it would be the "quickest" production vehicle to 60 miles per hour. On the half-pipe ramp, the vehicle was able to remain upside down due to a fan suction system. The air tanks in the vehicle are rechargeable and can be recompressed without fuel, according to Tesla. The vehicle uses compressed air to take off and land Long term, Musk said the car will be the "only manual" vehicle in its lineup, referencing plans for driverless vehicles . Though the demonstration used a pre-programmed sequence with no driver. Tesla chief designer Franz von Holzhausen said the car was designed with an "aerospace aesthetic". It has an angular supercar exterior with scissor doors and a deployable spoiler, and is a coupe with a hard top. Read: Videos reveal vertical takeoff of electric flying car in California The seats are moulded directly to the chassis, and it features wire steering, which replaces the mechanical link between the steering wheel and wheels with electronic controls. Musk referenced the uncertainty of street legality for the flying capabilities and said that " success is not guaranteed" before the test. The company gave it an "aerospace aesthetic" Production on the vehicle is set for 2028, according to Tesla. The company first unveiled a second-generation Roadster in 2017 , with deliveries planned for 2020. Tesla's last major launch was the Cybertruck , unveiled in 2019. Other recent concept cars include Alef's concept vehicle . The imagery is courtesy of Tesla. The post Tesla launches flying Roadster concept car appeared first on Dezeen .

Check it out ! “ coincidence ,” by K Bahr on Flickr “A coincidence, after all, has to be noticed.“ Dear friend of TAoN Suzanne M sent me a link the other day to a deep-dive article about coincidences . I’d never given this subject much thought, but it turned out to be pretty interesting. And as Suzanne detected, there was a noticing/attention angle that I couldn’t help dwelling on. A coincidence, after all, has to be noticed. If I walk past a childhood friend I haven’t seen in 20 years in some airport where neither of us lives, one of us has to notice the other for the coincidence to “count,” as it were. In some ways, “ the amazing thing is not that these things occur, it’s that we notice them, ” according to David Spiegelhalter, a professor at the University of Cambridge who studies such things, as quoted in Julie Beck’s’ Atlantic article. You could say that being more attentive leads to registering more coincidences. Spiegelhalter, the article notes, has a website where people can submit their coincidence experiences, and claims to have collected something like 5,000 of them. The most common form is “ finding a link with someone you meet .” Obviously, this suggests that people who are looking for connections — who are open, curious, attentive to others — are more likely to find unexpected ones. “Coincidences never happen to me at all, because I never notice anything,” Spiegelhalter says (somewhat jokingly). “I never talk to anybody on trains. If I’m with a stranger, I don’t try to find a connection with them … .” I admit it never really occurred to me that there could be coincidence-friendly types . But Beck also cites another researcher who has found that certain personality traits are linked to experiencing more coincidences—people who describe themselves as religious or spiritual, people who are self-referential (or likely to relate information from the external world back to themselves), and people who are high in meaning-seeking are all coincidence-prone. The article goes on to explore everything from Jung’s idea of synchronicity to popular notions of the paranormal. Possibly the opposite of missing coincidences is reading too much meaning into mere chance occurrences that look like something more. The world shapes our attention, but sometimes attention shapes our world — for better or worse! That said, I’m attracted to this idea that “finding a link with someone you meet” is the most-reported form of coincidence. It’s a nice frame for chatting with someone new: Be curious, be open — and look for a happy coincidence or two. Leave a comment Thank you Suzanne! Noticing is about other people, too. title: #305 | Offline é o novo hype (parte 2)
description: nas edições anteriores #303 | Marcas multiespécie #304 | Offline é o novo hype (parte 1) tempo de leitura: 4 minutos para entender 💡 Passamos os últimos dois anos falando, desejando, criando, repetindo o termo “offline” nos nossos planos de mídia e carrosseis de Instagram, a ponto dele ter se tornado também um grande hype . Por um lado, pessoas performando atividades online apenas para postar. Por outro, marcas usando esse movimento como desculpa pra poluir visualmente o mundo real ou encher as nossas casas de objetos desnecessários. (Nem tudo deveria ter um anúncio. O mundo não precisa de mais um brinde com o seu logo sem intenção nenhuma). E agora? _ Este não é um manifesto anti-offline. De maneira alguma. A gente não deve desistir de materializar as nossas marcas ou criar experiências no mundo real (não vamos desistir) . Mas neste processo, é importante entender duas coisas: 1. “Offline é o novo luxo” é uma maneira muito simplista de olhar para essa tendência. Ela é indiscutivelmente atrativa para as marcas de luxo, que sempre pautaram a sua comunicação na estética e estilos de vida capazes de diferenciar as pessoas. Quando a estética “comum” é cronicamente online, feita por IA e vidrada em uma tela, o luxo busca ilustrações feitas à mão e experiências sensoriais. Mas a necessidade de desconectar vai além da performance e da distinção social. O que torna o “offline” um movimento muito maior que qualquer trend é justamente a sua capacidade de resgatar uma série de aspectos que têm se perdido na vida moderna. A presença, a atenção, o processo, o aprendizado, a conexão com outras pessoas, a dificuldade (e, consequentemente, a resiliência)… E as tantas sensações, rituais e habilidades que só o mundo real proporciona. Objetos físicos, eventos e atividades manuais devem seguir parte da estratégia das marcas. Não para gerar percepção de luxo ou para fazer igual a uma ou outra. Muito menos para criar novos espaços de mídia que “chamam mais atenção”. E sim pela sua capacidade de interromper o scroll infinito, de ser um lembrete da vida que acontece fora das telas, de gerar valor e, quem sabe, até transformação real nas pessoas. O que nos leva ao segundo ponto. _ 2. Quando o offline se torna hype, é preciso fugir do lugar comum Em 2025, fizemos a primeira edição de uma revista impressa. Ela foi a realização de um sonho antigo, e a materialização da Bits to Brands em cores, ilustrações e páginas enviadas para todo o Brasil. Seu projeto editorial foi feito em outubro de 2024, e a sua impressão em dezembro. Na época, as revistas já começavam a despontar como símbolo de nostalgia - mas não dava para imaginar que seria um movimento tão intenso. Desde então, diversas marcas imprimiram revistas - e serviram café, receberam clubes do livro, ofereceram corridas de rua, distribuíram bonés bordados, estamparam câmeras analógicas… Assim, apenas na sua segunda edição, uma revista não é mais surpreendente ou inovadora. Do mesmo jeito que, em 2026, um boné também não é. (Aliás, um boné vira parte de uma coleção que está chegando a 20 unidades por aqui) O valor do offline não vai a lugar nenhum, mas fazer o básico não é mais o suficiente. O desafio é seguir se reinventando no mesmo formato. A boa notícia é que aí mora a diversão. Porque na tentativa de despertar o que há de mais humano em alguém (a presença, o contato, a memória), precisamos ser humanos primeiro . (criativos, sensíveis, curiosos). Fazer mais ou menos do mesmo jeito, mas um pouco diferente. Fazer mais ou menos a mesma coisa, mas fazer também algo novo. Tornar algo uma tradição, investir de fato em um ritual de marca - mas buscar novas formas de encontrar prazer no processo, e encantar as pessoas com o resultado. Uma revista, a gente já tinha feito. Um álbum de figurinhas foi a primeira vez. Vida longa à nossa imaginação e capacidade de reinvenção - bem humanas, e bem brasileiras :) _ A segunda edição da Revista Bits to Brands está no ar. Neste momento, ela está sendo presenteada para clientes e parceiros da Bits. Mas você vai poder garantir a sua. Na próxima edição da newsletter, dia 15/09, traremos todos os detalhes - e o link! Fiquem de olho porque a quantidade é limitada. Até lá, todos os detalhes estão sendo revelados aos poucos no nosso Instagram. :) para continuar a conversa nas redes sociais e convidar mais gente para cá, compartilhe usando o botão abaixo ou marcando a @bitstobrands Share para inspirar ✨ Essa campanha da Hermann Miller é um ótimo exemplo de como transformar um benefício funcional em conceito criativo. Porque uma cadeira de escritório não precisa querer salvar o mundo ou te fazer chorar com um anúncio. Ela é feita para você sentar melhor. E essa mensagem, com a execução certa, fica irresistível. para fazer parte da conversa 💬 O primeiro fim de semana do Rock in Rio foi marcado pela chuva - e pelas filas para pegar brindes nas ativações das marcas. Até agora, destacamos: O karaokê gigante do Itaú (por criar uma experiência memorável verdadeiramente integrada ao evento) A collab entre Uber e LATAM (por entenderem que, juntas, elas poderiam chamar mais atenção do que separadas) _ Para ficar de olho: hoje acontece o primeiro evento da Apple com o novo CEO , John Ternus, no comando. A expectativa é pelo celular dobrável da marca - que não oferece novidade, mas busca se destacar por design e performance. _ O Salesforce atualizou a sua identidade visual. Acredito no físico, no impresso e no analógico para muito além da trend ou do potencial de chamar atenção. Acredito tanto que, antes de falar, eu faço. E é fazendo - à mão, com calma, com muita troca e com todo o talento e entusiasmo de todos os envolvidos - que eu percebo o quanto isso tem valor. Um valor que não vai a lugar nenhum. title: #304 | Offline é o novo hype (parte 1)
description: nas edições anteriores #302 | Os oráculos da timeline #303 | Marcas multiespécie tempo de leitura: 5 minutos para entender 💡 Já vai fazer dois anos que a expressão “o offline é o novo luxo” se disseminou pela internet. Ora como análise de tendência, ora como sinalização de virtude. Nós também somos um pouco culpados disso: Em janeiro de 2025, prestes a lançar a primeira edição da nossa revista impressa, estávamos mergulhados no “offline”. E não só a gente. Foi um verão em que muita gente procurou desconectar, e assim seguiu pelas estações. De câmeras analógicas a aulas de cerâmica, palavras cruzadas, telefones fixos… Todo tipo de estratégia (e produto) foi surgindo para ajudar. Começando, inclusive, pelas marcas de luxo. Porque não é uma coincidência que este seja o adjetivo mais utilizado ao lado da palavra “offline”. Tanto porque o “luxo” é mais valioso e raro, quanto porque ele é aquilo que foge do comum. Quando uma estética ou comportamento se torna o básico, aquilo que todo mundo tem, beirando até o “brega” - performar superioridade intelectual e social é se afastar dela. (A relação entre consumo e performance social está super bem explicada em Coisa de Rico , de Michel Alcoforado). Se nos últimos anos o comum é ser hiperconectado, cronicamente online e passar incontáveis horas arrastando para cima imóvel, o que passa a comunicar luxo e status é desconectar. Ler livros de verdade, fazer atividade física ao ar livre, acessórios tecnológicos mais vintage, encontros para discutir temas específicos, o resgate dos hábitos e atividades sociais das avós (do tricô ao nonna-maxxing )… É por essas e outras que a Miu Miu tem um clube do livro, a Bottega Veneta lançou um jogo de Jenga, a Prada fez uma floricultura e as marcas de luxo têm disputado espaço para fazer ativações nos grandes torneios de tênis pelo mundo. O offline se tornou, sim, sinônimo de luxo. Mas não pára por aí. _ O offline se tornou território de desejo das marcas por motivos certos e errados, racionais e abstratos, mas muitos deles ancorados em comportamentos e demandas bem reais. Um deles é a distinção social. Mas ativações no mundo real, eventos, experiências e objetos físicos despertam interesse também porque são comunitários, sensoriais, duráveis, memoráveis e humanos. Cada um desses aspectos parte de demandas da vida contemporânea que começam no excesso de telas, mas se estendem para a ausência de interações sociais, a substituição do corpo físico pela imagem editada de alguém e até o tal “AI Slop”. Num parque a gente não precisa ficar se perguntando se algo é IA ou não a cada dois minutos (ainda). Porque o offline é comunidade , ele nos permite lembrar que não estamos sozinhos nos nossos gostos e hobbies - seja correr uma meia maratona, seja ter sido fã da Xuxa na infância. Porque o offline é sensorial , ele nos lembra que cada um é um corpo, e não apenas um cérebro e as pontas dos dedos. E que um corpo é capaz de sentir gostos, cheiros, toques, de dançar, cantar, esbarrar, ver e ser visto e se relacionar - de verdade. Porque o offline é durável , ele se torna representação no mundo real de quem a gente é. Aquilo que decora os nossos ambientes, que compõe as nossas coleções , que está pendurado nas nossas bolsas e mochilas ou até geladeiras - ajuda a contar a nossa história. Diga-me o que colecionas e te direi quem és. Porque o offline é memorável, ele é uma grande oportunidade para as marcas investirem seus orçamentos de comunicação de forma mais assertiva. Estamos descobrindo que reunir um grupo de pessoas verdadeiramente atentas e interessadas tem mais valor do que atingir milhões de views sabe-se lá de quem. E porque o offline é humano, ele é o único ambiente onde a gente vivencia o tempo de forma linear, a arte de forma artesanal e o mundo conforme a nossa própria curadoria de experiências - e não a de um algortimo. Não é à toa que todo mundo quer mais disso. _ Passamos os últimos dois anos falando, desejando, criando, repetindo o termo “offline” nos nossos planos de mídia e carrosseis de Instagram, a ponto dele ter se tornado também um grande hype . Por um lado, pessoas performando atividades online apenas para postar. Por outro, marcas usando esse movimento como desculpa pra poluir visualmente o mundo real ou encher as nossas casas de objetos desnecessários. (Nem tudo deveria ter um anúncio. O mundo não precisa de mais um brinde com o seu logo sem intenção nenhuma). E agora? _ continua na próxima edição. para continuar a conversa nas redes sociais e convidar mais gente para cá, compartilhe usando o botão abaixo ou marcando a @bitstobrands Share para inspirar ✨ Ao invés de só um case, vocês aceitam três? :) Como parte da nossa estratégia de ser verdadeiramente multicanal (com conteúdo feito para cada plataforma) e inspirar as pessoas por trás das marcas brasileiras e no Brasil, surgiu a #BrasilnaBits. Uma editoria no Instagram para explorar marcas brasileiras de diferentes regiões e segmentos, e tudo que elas têm a nos ensinar. Já passamos por Tramontina , Xeque Mate e Turma da Mônica . E se você tiver sugestões, pode deixar aqui nos comentários. para fazer parte da conversa 💬 O Instagram atualizou a sua tipografia e todo o seu universo visual . E é claro que todo mundo queria ter uma opinião. Convidamos Fábio Haag, um dos maiores especialistas em tipografia do Brasil (e do mundo), para dividir o seu olhar, no que muita gente considerou a melhor análise sobre o tema. Assista aqui. _ Na última semana, a cidade de São Paulo recebeu pela primeira vez o SP2B , evento de criatividade, inovação e negócios. Foram dias de grandes nomes, ótimas conversas e combinações inusitadas espalhadas por todo o Parque Ibirapuera - e na nossa timeline também . para ler com calma 📄 Criar cultura versus consumir tendências A “cultura do resumo” e para onde vai a nossa capacidade de pensar O mundo está ficando mais feio? “As coisas estão ficando maiores, mais barulhentas e mais insistentes visualmente - como se ocupar mais espaço fosse, por si só, uma forma de valor”. para mais conteúdo 📚 🖼️ siga a Bits no Instagram [link] 📚 confira uma seleção de livros na nossa biblioteca [link] 🎧 ouça o podcast Tudo que Importa [link] 🤝 anuncie na Bits - peça o nosso mídia kit em contato@bitstobrands.com 📩 assine essa newsletter , caso não tenha recebido por e-mail :) Subscribe now para dar um tchau 👋🏼 Quem estava aqui ano passado sabe - quando a gente começa a falar muito do mundo offline, é porque tem algo impresso vindo por aí. title: The Personal Brand Trap: Why Humans Shouldn’t Think of Themselves as Brands
description: When I was a wee little boy growing up, I wanted to be a fireman. It seemed considerably more achievable than becoming a ThunderCat or Batman, which were my other career choices when I was eight. At school I had absolutely no clue what I wanted to do as a career. Potentially something arty or sporty, but back in the 90s I was told neither of those were money-makers, so I had to think about getting a proper job. Today, I would classify myself as a designer and educator helping the next generation of creatives build more opportunity for themselves. That feels very aligned with who I am today. But I have also been a barman, factory worker, waiter, tattoo apprentice, window cleaner, failed businessman, unemployable bum, and many other things on the journey to finding this particular version of me. And that is one of the wonderful things about being a human… nobody really freaking knows who they’re going to become. The person you are today is probably very different from the person you were five years ago, and if you’re doing this thing called life properly, there’s a good chance the person you’ll become five years from now will look different again. And, from what my mum tells me… that’s completely normal. Most of us are making it up as we go, collecting experiences and continuously falling forward into newer versions of ourselves… we’re supposed to evolve. So in this little article I want to share my perspective on a topic that I think deserves a little more questioning: personal branding. More specifically, I want to explore why I don’t think humans should think of themselves as brands, and why applying brand logic to a human being can potentially do more harm than good. Thanks for reading The Real Brand Life! Subscribe for free to receive new posts. Now, I’m not here to suggest that personal branding doesn’t exist. That would cause a riot. Instead, I’d like to challenge some of the advice being peddled around willy-nilly on the dopamine drug train that is social media. To do that, I think we first need to agree on the difference between brand logic and human logic. A brand’s job is to reduce complexity. Brands are trying to be recognised at scale and for that to happen, they need to simplify things. They need to make themselves easier to understand, remember and choose. They do that better when they are associated with a couple of very clear ideas. Humans, on the other hand, operate very differently my friends. We change our minds all the freaking time. We become interested in new things. We learn stuff, we grow our minds and then we see the world differently because of it. And an important thing to add is that humans don’t naturally operate at scale. We evolved in small communities and tribes, not in front of thousands of random people online. So if brands become stronger through consistency and humans become stronger through change, are we really sure those two things belong together? That’s why I find phrases like “you are your brand” and “everyone has a personal brand” a little, well… problematic. Being known for something and being a brand are not the same thing. I understand that these phrases are often being used as shortcuts, but even when I account for that nuance, I still think they fundamentally misunderstand what a brand is… and what a human needs. Now, I don’t want this to come across as a rant or a black-and-white argument, as some of the advice coming out of the personal brand camp is incredibly useful. Visibility matters for sure because if nobody knows what the heck you do, how on earth are they supposed to hire you? Other people need to know you exist people. I absolutely believe humans should become known. Known for doing good work, having interesting ideas, standing for something and making a positive impact on the people around them. But becoming known and becoming a product are not the same thing. Being known, or what most would simply call a reputation, is something people gift you over time. It forms through your behaviour and the way you consistently show up for yourself. You don’t have to manufacture it, force it or spend every waking minute trying to manage how you’re perceived by others. A reputation happens naturally as you continue growing into the person you’re becoming. And this is where I think we can run into trouble because the moment we start thinking of ourselves as a brand, our focus can shift. Instead of asking, “Who am I becoming?” we start asking, “How will this look to other people?” The danger is that we start viewing ourselves through the eyes of an audience before we’ve had chance to fully understand ourselves… we start looking at ourselves from the outside in. At first, that might not sound like too much of a problem. In fact, it actually sounds pretty bloody sensible. If you’re running a business, surely you should care about how people feel when they see you. But I don’t believe growth and perception always want the same thing. The thing about growth is that it can look a bit messy from the outside. You change your mind, let go of old ideas and, more often than we’d like to admit, realise you got something wrong. That’s all part of the process. And brand logic doesn’t particularly reward that kind of thinking. Brands gain strength through their consistency. They keep showing up in roughly the same way until people know exactly what to expect from them. And I think that’s where a lot of people can run into a bit of an issue. The more successful a personal brand becomes, the more pressure there can be to keep being the person your audience already knows. To keep talking about the same things, showing up in the same way and feeding the machine that made people pay attention in the first place. That’s the personal brand trap. The human becomes responsible for holding onto a version of themselves they may have already outgrown. And as we see more people choosing freelance careers, building solo businesses and creating opportunities for themselves online, I think this becomes an increasingly important conversation to navigate. I know that perception matters, visibility matters, being known matters, and creating opportunity matters… but so does growth as a human being. Perhaps the challenge isn’t figuring out how to turn people into brands… instead it’s figuring out how to help people become known without trapping them. I’d hate to think that personal branding, the very thing so many people turn to in search of more opportunity, could end up becoming the thing that stops them from becoming who they’re supposed to be. So if I can leave you with a little bit of advice here it would be this: focus on the things you want to be known for, but don’t lose sight of the person you’re becoming along the way. Maybe the goal isn’t to manage perception at all. Perhaps it’s simply to become someone worth paying attention to. Humans are supposed to evolve. Brands are supposed to repeat. The problems arise when we start applying the rules of one to the other, so don’t flatten yourself into a product mindset just because the internet tells you that’s the secret to success. Focus on becoming known for your craft, your kindness and your character. Keep sharing what matters to you because opportunity has a funny way of finding people who do. Just please remember to sprinkle a little patience on yourself along the way. Your mate, James Thoughts on this? Comment below team. I’m excited to hear what you think. title: #300 | A vida das coisas
description: nas edições anteriores #298 | Cadê a conversão? #299 | Nesta Copa do Mundo, olhe em volta tempo de leitura: 4 minutos para entender 💡 “No jantar, um cirurgião me perguntou por que eu escrevo com uma caneta, ao invés de usar um ditafone ou processador de palavras. - Por que eu faria isso? - Porque é mais rápido e mais eficiente - Mas este é o trabalho da minha vida. Eu não tenho pressa”. Helen Garner, em 1984. _ “A Bits precisa ganhar vida…” foi uma frase muito repetida por aqui nos últimos meses. E, se vamos ser bem honestos, ela seguia com “...para além de mim” . Nas muitas folhas de papel em que cenários foram desenhados, era como se até aqui a Bits precisasse da Beatriz para existir - e era chegado o momento da sua independência. Pensem numa dor de crescimento. Maravilhosa, pois em oito anos a gente cresceu muito . Mas não menos doída. A Bits to Brands se tornou uma empresa antes que “empreender” se tornasse uma habilidade por aqui. Uma conversa que a creator economy adora evitar, essa de que viver de conteúdo é mais estruturar processos e fluxos de caixa do que ter ideias brilhantes que podem viralizar. Mais economy , menos creator . Enquanto tenta vender produtos que mudam o tempo inteiro, para clientes que pagam em 90 dias, com um big boss que oscila as suas métricas sem nenhuma lógica aparente. Coisa de gente meio maluca. Mas um dia você cria algo despretensiosamente, e aos poucos aquilo vai ganhando vida até que a sua existência se torna inegociável. Aí você negocia a sua rotina como CLT, o seu planejamento financeiro, as suas habilidades, o que significa “horário comercial”. Negocia os seus valores, seus limites, suas parcerias. E segue. _ 300 edições depois, há todo um planejamento estratégico baseado na capacidade de enxergar a Bits to Brands não mais como quem olha no espelho, mas como quem encara o horizonte. Porque a Bits é o trabalho da minha vida, mas eu sou apenas uma parte da vida dela. Nos grandes marcos até aqui, as reflexões sempre foram sobre o processo de criar, de começar, de continuar. Hoje, eu escolho celebrar o infinito do que vai além. Certamente muita coisa começa no som do teclado em uma noite silenciosa, ou num áudio animado com uma ideia que parece absurda. Só que incrível mesmo é o que acontece depois. Anos atrás, um garoto no interior do Mato Grosso leu centenas de edições do arquivo de uma newsletter e aquilo foi essencial pra que ele decidisse seguir carreira em comunicação. Hoje, ele trabalha na WPP. Há pouco mais de uma semana, uma mulher foi oficialmente contratada como professora de pós-graduação por causa de uma conversa que começou em um grupo de Whatsapp chamado “Comunidade Bits” . Tem também a dona de um café em Joinville que, na época do lançamento de Barbie, viu um post no Instagram da Bits sobre o hype de produtos com a cara do filme. Pois ela fez um bolinho rosa temático - e esgotou todas as unidades. Outro dia, chegando num grande evento para palestrar, uma moça se levantou da primeira fila e tirou da bolsa uma revista da Bits, que ela ganhou porque indicou a sua newsletter favorita para dezenas de pessoas, e guarda até hoje como algo especial. _ O “agora” exerce uma pressão imensa sobre a gente, o tempo todo. O formato em alta, o calendário de posts da semana, o assunto mais comentado do momento, a mais nova ferramenta de IA que vai fazer tudo por você. E a roda não para nunca de girar - há 300 edições e contando. Mas não dá para perder de vista tudo que acontece quando a gente cria algo, e aquilo que a gente cria ganha vida na vida de alguém. De maneira totalmente imprevisível, incontrolável e muitas vezes até irreversível. Como são todas as coisas grandiosas, e todas as coisas pequenas também. title: Default Bias: Who chose your settings?
description: When a choice arrives with one option already set, most people leave it in place, regardless of whether it reflects their actual preference. The friction of changing something, combined with the implicit signal that the pre-set option is normal or recommended, produces consistent gravity toward the status quo. The mechanism runs through several channels at once. Loss aversion makes changing a default feel like risking something already owned. Implied endorsement suggests the default is a reasonable choice, so selecting it requires less justification. And the cognitive cost of evaluating alternatives encourages people to accept the existing state. These forces compound, especially in low-stakes or unfamiliar decisions where people lack strong preferences to override them. Default bias appears across organ donation programs, retirement savings enrollment, privacy settings, and software configuration. In each case, the same population of people produces dramatically different outcomes depending on which option requires action and which requires inaction. The default does not just simplify the interface. It determines the outcome for a large share of users. In design A user opens a new account and immediately lands in a signup flow. Before they have formed any preferences, the product has already decided: marketing emails are on, data sharing is enabled, notifications fire at full volume. The user clicks through, and the defaults stay. Default bias means the designer’s pre-set choices become most users’ permanent choices, whether or not those choices were made with the user’s benefit in mind. This places significant weight on the moment a default is chosen. Every pre-selected option is effectively a policy decision applied to the full user base. Designers who understand this use defaults to serve the majority, while keeping alternatives reachable. Those who ignore it discover that their defaults reflect internal convenience or business incentives rather than user needs. Applications in digital products Set the default communication preference to the least intrusive option, then let users escalate: email digests before individual notifications, not the reverse. When offering a free-to-paid upgrade, pre-select the plan that fits the user’s current usage, not the highest-tier plan, so the default reflects their situation. Place the destructive or irreversible action as the non-default: require an affirmative click to delete, unsubscribe, or share data, rather than treating those as pre-selected states. In onboarding forms, default empty fields to blank rather than placeholder values that users might submit without reading. On privacy and data settings, default to the most private configuration and present expansion as a deliberate user choice, not a correction of a setting they already “agreed to.” When a setting has a best-fit value for most users, pre-select it with a visible label like “Recommended” so the default carries transparent reasoning rather than hidden authority. Industry examples Countries with automatic organ donation enrollment see consent rates above 90%. Countries that require a positive registration act see rates below 20%. Same populations, different defaults. Thaler and Benartzi documented a similar pattern in 401(k) enrollment in 2003. Companies that switched retirement plans to automatic enrollment saw participation jump from around 50% to over 90%. Employees could still remove themselves. Most did not. Microsoft pre-selected telemetry and automatic update settings in Windows 10 that collected substantial user data. Changing them required navigating several menus. Few users did. Google enabled AI-assisted email completion in Gmail by default for all users. Adoption was high not because users chose it, but because disabling it required a deliberate action most skipped. Apple’s App Tracking Transparency, released in 2021, shifted ad tracking from an on-by-default state to an explicit prompt. Consent rates dropped from an estimated 70% to under 30%. No one changes what they don’t notice Changing a default requires two things most people avoid at the same time: forming a preference and acting on it. The pre-set option eliminates both requirements. People accept it without deliberating, often without noticing the choice was made. This is not a failure of attention, rather a rational response to cognitive load . When a decision is low-salience and the default seems reasonable, the cost of evaluating alternatives outweighs the benefit. The designer who sets the default has, in effect, already made the decision for the majority. This is why defaults carry ethical weight. A designer can claim to offer choice while structuring the choice so that most users never exercise it. Defaults are most powerful in one-time setup flows, where users move quickly and rarely return to revisit. Designers who want users to engage with settings should surface them at the moment of relevance, not bury them in preferences menus users open once and forget. Choosing the default is unavoidable. There is no neutral pre-selection. Every product that ships with a setting in place has already made a choice about whose interests that setting serves. Further reading The Power of Defaults — Jakob Nielsen, Nielsen Norman Group (2005) Defaults — The Decision Lab Status Quo Bias — The Decision Lab Choice Architecture 2.0: How People Interpret and Make Sense of Nudges — Job Krijnen, Behavioral Scientist (2018) Defaults Are Not the Same by Default — Jachimowicz, Duncan, Weber, and Johnson, Behavioral Scientist (2019) You just read why the pre-set option wins. So here’s one I’ve set for you: The reference designers keep open. Default Bias is 1 of 106 principles in Psychology of Design; the complete reference behind this newsletter. What attention does. How trust forms. Why habits stick. Each one written the way you just read this one: the mechanism, where it shows up, and how to use it.
