title: Snøhetta completes landmark opera house in Shanghai
description: A giant spiral staircase guides visitors to the roof of the Shanghai Grand Opera House, which international studio Snøhetta designed to be "as much a civic destination as a performance venue". Located on the Huangpu River waterfront in Shanghai, China, the 146,786-square-metre opera house was conceived as a major cultural landmark that can accommodate a variety of musical performances. Snøhetta has completed the Shanghai Grand Opera House While Snøhetta 's design responds to a highly ambitious brief, the studio said it began the project as it always does, by taking time to examine and understand the specific site and its context, no matter the scale. According to the studio, this helped it to create the desired landmark while ensuring it felt like an extension of the existing public realm, open and accessible to both ticket holders and passersby. It is located on the Huangpu River waterfront "We always begin the same way, regardless of scale: by understanding the context," Snøhetta co-founder Kjetil Thorsen told Dezeen. "A cultural building, any building for that matter, must respond to its surroundings, the people who use it, the performers it serves, and the city it becomes part of," he reflected. "When I last visited the site, I was asked by a Chinese architecture student how we managed to create a building that felt so Chinese despite not being from China. The answer lies in observation and understanding context." Its key feature is a giant spiral staircase Shanghai Grand Opera House's defining feature is its spiral staircase, which dramatically cantilevers at its peak and was intended to emulate everything from an unfolding fan to a dancer or a set of piano keys. It leads directly to the publicly accessible rooftop, which doubles as a stage, an observation deck or simply a meeting point. According to Thorsen, it was integral to making the building feel part of the urban fabric. The staircase has a dramatic cantilever He compared the design to the Oslo Opera House , which the studio completed in 2000, with both designs actively seeking to "reduce thresholds wherever possible". "Buildings like opera houses inevitably create thresholds through walls, doors, and ticketed programs. We see it as our responsibility to challenge those thresholds and make the building as much a civic destination as a performance venue," Thorsen explained. "People should be able to enjoy the building without attending a performance. It should become part of everyday life, a place to spend time, meet others, and experience the city," he added. "A successful landmark is not only recognised by visitors, it is also embraced by the people who live around it and make it part of their everyday lives." The lobby is designed to feel light and open Shanghai Grand Opera House has a radial plan and contains a trio of auditoriums alongside exhibition and education spaces, restaurants and rehearsal and production areas. The facade flits between transparent and opaque finishes, depending on where the studio wanted to provide privacy and openness. For example, expansive glass elements maximise natural light and views in the lobby. The main auditorium has five levels Together, the three auditoriums can accommodate 4,200 people and host a range of performances. The main auditorium, called the Harmony Hall, contains 2,000 seats across its five levels, while the second hall, named the Soar Theatre, is more intimate, with space for 1,200 people. The final auditorium contains 1,000 seats and was constructed as a highly flexible space with adaptive seating and staging, catering to more experimental performances. It is fronted with a large glass facade overlooking the river. "For younger generations especially, that flexibility can help make cultural experiences feel more relevant, accessible, and connected to contemporary life," said Thorsen. Read: Snøhetta's Oslo Opera House was the most significant building of 2007 Shanghai Grand Opera House's material palette is a play of contrasts, with the light-coloured white stone, glass, and timber exterior having a more open feel than the darker, more intimate interiors. Inside, the auditoriums each have a unique aesthetic. The main hall is filled with deep red tones and surfaces, intended to feel as though they are carved from a single block, while lighter wooden materials characterise the other two. At night, the stage towers that project from the building are illuminated, shifting in colour to "animate the roof and the skyline". The smallest performance hall is designed to be adaptive Minimising the building's carbon footprint was a significant challenge due to the building's "scale and complexity", Thorsen said, but this was achieved through measures including passive design strategies. The bright roof reflects sunlight and heat rather than absorbing it, and the public lobby opens towards both the river and the park, allowing for cross-ventilation. A palette of durable materials and an adaptable interior will ensure a long lifespan for the building, while a close connection to public transport minimises dependence on private vehicles. Shanghai Grand Opera House is complete with a landscape design that connects to existing parkland, wetlands and public spaces to support local biodiversity and provide ample public space. The other auditorium accommodates 1,200 guests Snøhetta was founded by Thorsen and Craig Dykers in 1989. It won an international competition to design the opera house in 2016 and developed it with the state-owned firm East China Architectural Design & Research Institute (ECADI) and consultants Theatre Projects and Nagata Acoustics . Other major cultural projects by the studio include the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library in North Dakota and the rippled Glasshouse Theatre in Queensland . title: Baird Architects releases first furniture collection as "natural extension" of studio
description: US architecture studio Baird Architects has released its inaugural furniture collection, with seating, tables, and shelving, designed by in-house architects and collaborators and made in Portugal. The twelve-piece BA Objeto collection was led by Baird Architects founder Matthew Baird, who designed several pieces and also commissioned studio employees and collaborators. Each piece is credited to its designer, and the designers will receive a portion of the profits, according to Baird. Ines Gulbenkian designed an aluminium coffee table for the Ba Objeto collection The works include a solid walnut "surf" table by Baird, a swooping aluminium coffee table by Ines Gulbenkian and a dark brown cork bench by Gina Jiang. The pieces are primarily produced in Lisbon , Portugal, where Baird Architects has established a new studio to support its furniture making. Baird said a "considered approach to materiality, a crisp aesthetic, and a desire to push the boundaries of furniture design" draws the collection together. Gina Jiang created a cork made of a dark brown cork material The move points to an expansion of the studio's work beyond one-off furniture creation and illustrates a different business model for architecture studios. "Furniture feels like a natural extension of our architectural practice because it allows us to explore our interests in materiality, form, and craftsmanship at a more intimate scale," Baird told Dezeen. "We also wanted to create something that celebrates the individual designers within our studio, giving them the freedom to develop pieces of their own while contributing to a collective endeavour." Read: Apparatus draws on Persian mythology for its first full collection in five years Other pieces in the collection include a mirror by Portuguese designer Teresa Mascarenhas and a plywood and leather chair by designer Katy Cheng. Baird said the collection is an extension of the furniture the studio has created for private clients over the years, and that the team is already "looking ahead" to a second collection. Baird Architects commissioned Portuguese architect Teresa Mascarenha for the project From design fairs to heritage brands, designers and architects are currently attempting to restructure business models in the design world, primarily to receive more profit and credit for their work. Recently, Dezeen spoke with design companies OMHU and Rarify about their unique business models and outlooks that aspire to change the industry. title: Spaces by Manah signposts Chennai community centre with barrel-vaulted roof
description: Local architecture studio Spaces by Manah has completed The Soil & Sea community centre in Chennai, India , with a brick barrel-vaulted roof that serves as a "visible landmark" on the site. The 4,330-square-metre building was designed to provide learning space for a local education centre, as well as to house community workshops and events. Spaces by Manah designed its single-storey masonry structure to appear as though it were "growing out of the existing landscape", creating a series of outdoor and open-air spaces that overlook its lush surroundings. Spaces by Manah has completed a community centre in Chennai, India "The project sits within a lush, tree-lined parcel of land with the design growing out of the existing landscape," the studio told Dezeen. "The building is positioned to retain its connection with the trees and outdoor spaces through a sequence of shaded, open and enclosed spaces, while the dominant barrel vault rises above the canopy to create a visible landmark within the site," it added. Raised on a rubble stone foundation, the centre is organised around a flat-roofed volume, flanked on two sides by an L-shaped verandah that was conceived by the studio as an "intermediate, informal zone" between the building and landscape. A barrel-vaulted roof crowns the gathering space Steps and a ramp at the building's front lead up to the verandah, which is sheltered by the barrel-vaulted roof on one side to form a main gathering space for the community. Meanwhile, its other edge is topped with a sloping, tiled roof. A series of granite stone pillars frame the space, along with built-in seating. Read: Sculptural music centre shows bamboo as "a serious construction material" "The architecture responds to this idea through a strong central gathering space, expressed by the barrel vault, with more intimate and informal spaces arranged around it," the studio said. "An L-shaped veranda acts as an intermediate, informal zone between the enclosed spaces and the landscape, with built-in seating and ramps supporting movement, accessibility and interaction throughout the building." Granite stone pillars and Mangalore tiles complement the building's brick walls The bricks used for the structure's load-bearing walls were left exposed throughout the space. To complement the brick design, the studio sourced doors, windows and Mangalore floor tiles locally and repurposed them throughout the building. This materiality extends to the building's interior, where exposed brick walls and roof elements are set off by glossy tiles. "The material palette was intentionally kept natural, tactile and largely raw, allowing the building to sit comfortably within its landscape," the studio said. Glossy tiles are used within the interior Also on the site is a separate toilet block, which is similarly perched atop a stone foundation, and complete with load-bearing brick walls and a tiled canopy roof. Elsewhere in Chennai, Ekarth Studio has used bamboo to form a sculptural venue for the Maestro Ilaiyaraaja Centre for Music Learning and Research , while Habitat Collaborative has threaded a curved school through a tree-filled site in Vadodara . title: Factory in Bangladesh that "redefines manufacturing architecture" wins RIBA International Prize
description: A rug factory in Rangpur, Bangladesh , designed by Dhaka-based studio Nakshabid Architects to dismantle workplace hierarchies, has won the RIBA International Prize for 2026. Named Green Field Factory, the project is the fifth winner of the biennial award, presented by the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) to the world's best new building outside the UK. Nakshabid Architects was praised by the RIBA jury for designing a factory that incorporates passive design principles and prioritises the wellbeing of its 5,000 employees. Green Field Factory won this year's RIBA International Prize. Photo by City Syntax "Green Field Factory redefines manufacturing architecture in South Asia and beyond," said RIBA president Christ Williamson. "By putting people, wellbeing and their everyday experiences at its core and actively supporting its female workforce, it proves that thoughtful design can dismantle traditional hierarchies to create profound social and environmental change." It was announced as the RIBA International Prize winner at the Stirling Prize ceremony in London last night. This year's prestigious Stirling Prize was given to Mary Duggan Architects and Ruff Architects for the Lion Green Road housing development in London. The factory has a monumental green wall. Photo by City Syntax Commissioned by rug manufacturer Karupannya Rangpur Limited , Green Field Factory is a seven-storey building surrounded by fields and small settlements. Nakshabid Architects based the design on the traditional Bengali home, incorporating natural ventilation and biophilic design principles. Courtyards, verandas, gardens and a monumental green facade were designed to let natural light and airflow into the building, minimising the need for mechanical systems. Nakshabid Architects designed the building with passive ventilation. Photo by Prantography Green Field Factory has one main entrance with two grand staircases for all workers, intended to challenge hierarchies in the workplace. This responds to other factories in the area that have separate entrances for factory workers and people in management roles. Shared spaces in the factory provide areas for workers to take breaks and socialise. Other areas are designated to support workers' families and the wider community during the day and outside of working hours, including a rooftop daycare centre, on-site medical practice, grocery shop and prayer room. A connection to nature is provided through low-maintenance planting throughout, which also supports insects and birds, while artwork and sculptures celebrate the role of women in the workplace, family and community. Read: "Welcoming and inclusive" London housing wins RIBA Stirling Prize 2026 "The project demonstrates the dissolution of architecture as a topological space, with a single-pointed focus on dismantling civilisational oppression and hierarchy, for woman and man alike," said grand jury chair Bijoy Jain. "Through the simple gesture of two grand stairs as an equanimous shared portal, it transforms a space and symbol once reserved exclusively for the king of the region, as landlord and ruling class, and for the colonial power that pervaded the length and breadth of the country," he continued. "The architect and owner shared how the women and men working in the factory would bring their families with pride to show them where they worked, and the women empowered in their self-reliance to take life and familial decisions on their own." The jury praised the design for prioritising the wellbeing of the factory employees. Photo by Karupannya Rangpur The RIBA International Prize is awarded biennially to a building that "demonstrates visionary, innovative thinking, and design excellence whilst making a distinct contribution for its users and within its physical context". Green Field Factory was selected ahead of BRAC University in Bangladesh by WOHA, Z33 art museum in Belgium by Francesca Torzo Architetto and the renovation of Royale Belge in Belgium by Caruso St John Architects, Bovenbouw Architectuur and DDS+. YIMBY by Maker Architecten was named the winner of the International Emerging Architect Award. Photo by Stijn Bollaert Alongside the International Prize, RIBA awarded this year's International Emerging Architect Award to Maker Architecten for its YIMBY residential project in Kortrijk, Belgium. The project revamped 18 plots across a 1920's garden city neighbourhood, utilising reclaimed materials for new facades and creating communal green space. In 2024, Peris + Toral Arquitectes won the RIBA International Prize for an "inclusive and sustainable" social housing project in Barcelona. The top photo is by Mud Canvas. title: "Welcoming and inclusive" London housing wins RIBA Stirling Prize 2026
description: The Lion Green Road housing in south London, designed by local studios Mary Duggan Architects with Ruff Architects, has won this year's RIBA Stirling Prize for the UK's best new building. Located in Coulsdon, the high-density development commissioned by Croydon Council provides 157 homes across five blocks, which are stitched together by a series of shared green spaces. Lion Green Road has won the RIBA Stirling Prize 2026 The Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) named the project as winner of the prestigious prize at a ceremony in London this evening. It is the fourth housing scheme to win the prize since its inception 30 years ago, following Accordia in Cambridge in 2008, Goldsmith Street in Norwich in 2019 and Appleby Blue Almshouse in London in 2025. The development comprises five blocks staggered across a sloped site. Photo by RIBA The jury hailed Mary Duggan Architects and Ruff Architects for "addressing the pressing need for national housing" and providing environmentally considerate homes with ample access to light, nature and community. "More than a housing development, the scheme has created a welcoming and inclusive place where people can connect with one another, and with nature," read the citation. Lion Green Road comprises five blocks with a mix of private and socially rented homes. They are staggered across its steeply sloped site – a topographically challenging plot previously used as a car park. The blocks have faceted, star-shaped plans, which are rotated to offer unique views across the landscape and ensure each home is dual-aspect, maximising natural light. The blocks are unified by three different brick types A trio of complementary brick types clad the buildings, helping to visually unify them while giving each its own unique aesthetic. Shared outdoor spaces that weave through the blocks enhance this unification, giving residents opportunities to meet and engage with each other. RIBA said the project addresses "the pressing need for national housing" RIBA president Chris Williamson said the scheme demonstrates how high-density housing "can be achieved without compromising the quality of the places we create". "Through a consistent specification, with subtle variation in height and orientation, it offers housing at scale without uniformity," he reflected. "The architects have created a new kind of garden neighbourhood that balances privacy and generous views with a strong connection to nature – it's a living landscape," Williamson continued. "This is thoughtful, resourceful architecture that proves that even the most challenging of sites can be transformed into truly distinctive places for people to call home." Read: "Hopeful and imaginative" social housing wins RIBA Stirling Prize 2025 The RIBA Stirling Prize has been awarded annually to the UK's best new building since 1996. Lion Green Road was chosen from a six-strong shortlist, revealed in July . It was announced as this year's winner at a ceremony at Old Billingsgate this evening, where RIBA also revealed the recipients of its five Special Awards. This included the RIBA Neave Brown Award for Housing, which was won by Satish Jassal Architects for Rowan Court , a cluster of brick-clad social housing blocks in Seven Sisters. Collaborators Samuel Chisholm Studio and Takero Shimazaki took home the RIBA Reinvention Award for Oru Sutton, a co-working space in an old department store, while Tonkin Liu Architects won the RIBA Client of the Year Award in recognition of the York Minster Centre of Excellence. Finally, the RIBA Conservation Award was given to Architectural Thread for The Buttermarket, an arts-focused community hub in Cornwall, which also won the RIBA Stephen Lawrence Prize for emerging architectural talent. Green spaces are woven through the site. Photo by RIBA Previous winners of the Stirling Prize include London's Elizabeth Line in 2024, The New Library at Magdalene College in 2022 and a seaside pier in Hastings in 2017. Last year's award, which was won by the "hopeful and imaginative" Appleby Blue Almshouse social housing , sparked concerns about London bias , with four of the six shortlisted buildings located in the capital city. Earlier this year, the shortlist for the 2026 Stirling Prize was a topic of conversation in our Dezeen Weekly podcast, with our journalists pondering if architecture has become too boring . title: What is "the gravity of average" and why is it holding you back?
description: I grew up believing one thing: Don’t be average. Looking back now, as an older, slightly fatter man, there’s something wonderfully ironic about that particular piece of advice. While every person in authority was telling me not to become average, the systems around me were teaching me exactly how to become it. School teaches us there was one right answer. Business teaches us there’s a right process. Algorithms tell us there’s a right format. Most industries have their own best practices, and society at large constantly reminds us that fitting in is safer than standing out. None of these proven systems are bad. In fact, they’re incredibly useful. They help us educate millions of little people, build reliable businesses, and make sense of an increasingly complicated world. But when you start stacking them on top of one another, year after year, decade after decade… something intriguing happens. They all pull us in the exact same direction: Toward what’s proven Toward what’s predictable Toward what’s familiar Toward the flipping middle We hear a lot these days about falling test scores, declining creativity, and a lack of ambition. I’m not convinced that’s the whole story. I think we’re living inside an ecosystem of invisible forces that constantly reward the safest path. Millions of perfectly sensible decisions, made by perfectly sensible people, combine to suck us toward the same ideas until we all end up in the exact same place… the fookin’ middle. I call this: the gravity of average. Whether we realize it or not, we’ve been caught in its invisible pull since the day we were born… damn it. Here are the five layers of gravity conspiring against us all, and why you need to fight them with everything you’ve got to protect your individual magic. 1. Educational gravity Our first experience of this gravity starts in the classroom. School has an incredibly difficult job: educating millions of children fairly and consistently, often with limited resources and enormous expectations. The only way to make that possible is to rely on standardized curricula, rigid grading schemes, and easily measured outcomes. From a very young age, we learn to optimize for what gets rewarded … the gold stars, the praise from teachers, the good-old pats on the back. Before long, we’re no longer just learning the subject, we’re learning how to succeed within the system. The educational environment doesn’t intentionally produce average people. Far from it. But when success is measured in the exact same way for everyone, it’s only natural that millions of children begin chasing the exact same things. The more people optimize for the identical outcome, the more they will eventually look alike… it’s the logical outcome of a predictable system. 2. Economic gravity Businesses only exist if they survive, and to do that, they have to make rational decisions. If a pricing model has worked before, why change it? If a marketing strategy has proven successful, why reinvent it? If a competitor is growing using a particular approach, it’s only natural to copy it. None of these are bad decisions. Economist Harold Hotelling described this exact phenomenon in what became known as Hotelling’s Law . When businesses compete for the same customers, they naturally drift toward one another rather than away. Differentiation feels risky, while similarity feels sensible. Over time, this way of thinking compounds. What starts as “best practice” gradually becomes the default way of doing business. When an entire industry chases the identical measures of success (revenue, profit, or market share), even the most original business ideas eventually drift toward the average when they optimize for the same thing. 3. Social gravity As humans, we’ve always worried about belonging. For most of human history, being accepted by the group dramatically increased our chances of not becoming dead. That instinct is still hardwired into us. One of my favourite psychology experiments that backs this up comes from Solomon Asch . Participants were invited into a room to complete what they thought was a simple test about the length of a few lines. What they didn’t know was that everyone else in the room was an actor hired to be in on the experiment. The answers were obvious, but one by one, the actors deliberately gave the wrong answer. Faced with an entire room disagreeing with them, many participants ignored what they could clearly see and went along with the crowd instead. Around 75% of people conformed at least once, even though the group was clearly wrong. Nobody has to tell us to fit in. We just learn which parts of ourselves earn acceptance and which parts are safer left hidden. 4. Algorithmic gravity Welcome to the newest kid on the block. Algorithms don’t care about “silly” things like originality… all they give a poop about is retention. The easiest way to predict what will keep your attention is to look at what has already worked. Successful ideas become recommendations. Recommendations become trends. Trends become the templates that every influencer and their dog starts copying. Before long, thousands of people are creating different versions of the exact same thing because that’s what the system keeps serving up. Social media isn’t in the business of finding the next brilliant idea. It’s in the business of keeping us scrolling, and scrolling, and scrolling. And the easiest way to do that is by feeding us a slightly repackaged version of the average… the baseline of everything the system has already gobbled up before. 5. Professional gravity Every profession develops its own “playbook.” Designers have processes, marketers have foolproof plans, and consultants have their frameworks. Most of these defaults exist because someone, at some point, solved a real problem for a real person… hurrah. The danger happens when best practice subtly becomes the only practice. The longer an approach survives unquestioned, the more it feels like common sense. Before long, entire industries are repeating formulas that worked 30 years ago, even though the world has completely evolved around them. The comfort zone is a very dangerous place. Nothing grows there, as they say. The optimization trap What I’ve realized about these five forces is that they all share the exact same mischievous mechanism. Every system must decide what success looks like and, once it does, the rest of us naturally optimize for it. School rewards grades. Business rewards revenue. Algorithms reward engagement. Society rewards acceptance. Professions reward best practice. None of the above are bad… but when millions of people chase the exact same measures of success, gravity takes over. Human beings are remarkably good at adapting to their environment. The more we align ourselves with the same definition of success, the more we begin to resemble one another. And today, more people than ever are finding themselves in the middle. For most of history, becoming competent at something took years of deliberate practice. Today, technology can get almost anyone to “good enough” in a matter of minutes. Technology is closing the gap from below, while optimization is closing the gap from above. People who once struggled to produce competent work can now create something perfectly passable with better tools. At the same time, many of the people who were once exceptional are handing more of their thinking over to those same tools. In the pursuit of speed they often sacrifice the originality and personality that made them stand out in the first place. One force lifts people into the middle. The other pulls people back towards it. Now, there is absolutely nothing wrong with being average. Millions of people build fulfilling careers, do meaningful work, and live brilliant lives without ever trying to stand out. But commercially, today, average is becoming a far riskier place to build a future. To riff on something Rory Sutherland once said: when you become logical, you become predictable. And when you become predictable, you become replaceable. That doesn’t mean you should reject logic or stop using new technology. It simply means those things are no longer enough. They help you meet the standard, yes, but they’ll never make you the obvious choice. I’ve come to believe that opportunity doesn’t flow toward the middle. It flows toward recognizable differences that people trust. The gravity of average never disappears. You simply decide whether to drift with it… or spend your time pushing against it. Maybe that’s what Mr. Hotelling was trying to tell us all along. Test the edges. - James This article first appeared in my Fast Company column. You can check it out here .

description: nas edições anteriores #299 | Nesta Copa do Mundo, olhe em volta #300 | A vida das coisas tempo de leitura: 5 minutos para entender 💡 Às vésperas da Copa do Mundo, em 2022, comentamos na edição 188 que era a primeira Copa pós-TikTok e a primeira Copa pós-Casimiro. Quatro anos depois, a Copa de 2026 trouxe outras primeiras vezes, que certamente vão criar novas dinâmicas para marcas, fãs e espectadores. Essa é a primeira Copa pós-inteligência artificial generativa. O que se refletiu em feeds lotados de conteúdo em tempo real durante os jogos (a CazéTV, por exemplo, soltou dezenas de posts sobre o Cristiano Ronaldo em minutos), e deepfakes de jogadores em situações inusitadas. Um ponto de atenção aqui é ver uma tecnologia tão potencialmente perigosa se tornar apenas engraçada quando utilizada, por exemplo, para recriar uma cena de As Branquelas com Vini Jr. e Erling Haaland. E o momento, que parecia ideal para sua consolidação definitiva e ganho de credibilidade, teve efeito contrário. As marcas de bet se tornaram tóxicas para as transmissões que patrocinaram, atrapalhando a experiência dos espectadores e gerando antipatia a todos os envolvidos. O canal, o narrador, a marca, até os jogadores. E é além de entretenimento. 61% das apostas sugeridas pela CazéTV foram perdidas. Eis um novo universo de interação e entretenimento na internet: a tradução automática de posts na timeline do Twitter (X). Colocada no ar em março de 2026, bem a tempo. Basicamente, essa feature faz com que tweets escritos em qualquer idioma apareçam na sua timeline em português. Existe uma sinalização discreta da tradução, mas a experiência é fluida - você passa por aquele comentário como se ele estivesse realmente no seu contexto. E contexto é chave aqui, porque agora quem fala pode ser compreendido em toda a sua espontaneidade, sem precisar adaptar as suas palavras a quem ouve. Como naquele episódio clássico de Modern Family, em que a personagem de Sofia Vergara, uma mulher latina, se frustra com o marido americano porque não consegue transmitir toda a sua personalidade em inglês. “Você sabe o quão frustrante é ter que traduzir tudo na minha cabeça antes de falar? Você sabe o quão inteligente eu sou em espanhol?” Todo mundo que já tentou se comunicar em um outro idioma entende o que ela quer dizer. Nós somos naturalmente mais espontâneos onde temos mais fluência. Voltando ao Twitter (X), é justamente a espontaneidade e a total fluência do brasileiro em memes que agora começam a se espalhar pelo mundo - um post traduzido de cada vez. Nesta Copa do Mundo, um francês e um brasileiro puderam discutir como se estivessem na mesma mesa de bar, se entendendo plenamente. E bom… se ofendendo, também. Com destaque para a rixa imaginária entre o técnico Ancelotti e Endrick, que foi ganhando forma nas situações mais absurdas. Isso viralizou a ponto de uma marca europeia entrar na conversa. O que inaugura uma nova era de interação nas redes sociais: o seu social listening agora é global. Porque o Twitter é só o começo. title: #299 | Nesta Copa do Mundo, olhe em volta
description: nas edições anteriores #297 | Escolher o caminho difícil #298 | Cadê a conversão? tempo de leitura: 4 minutos para entender 💡 Eu sempre vivi rodeada por futebol. A TV ligada passando o jogo aos fins de semana, o jornal esportivo local todos os dias no almoço, as idas ao estádio do Figueirense com o meu pai, e depois com meu marido. A imagem de um jogo de futebol é muito presente nas minhas lembranças, e na TV aqui em casa até hoje. Como deve ser para muita gente também. O meu nível de interesse pelo esporte em si oscilou no decorrer da vida, até chegar, hoje, em uma certa apatia. Quando tem um jogo passando numa quarta-feira à noite, eu já não faço a menor ideia de qual o torneio ou quem está em campo. Mas os anos trabalhando com marcas e observando o mundo em uma busca constante de pontos para conectar e análises para fazer, levaram o meu olhar para outro canto da televisão. Lembro bem do dia em que passei mergulhada em um conteúdo sobre o branding das bets no Brasil , e a partida de futebol à noite foi mais um “sinal”. Ignorando totalmente os lances, me desafiei a contar: quantas marcas de bet tem aqui? Nove. Isso era 2024. A transmissão de uma partida de futebol é um reflexo dos tempos em que vivemos. Porque o time em campo é protagonista, mas as marcas à sua volta contam uma outra história - sobre consumo, mídia e sociedade. O auge disso, claro, é a Copa do Mundo. _ Em 1958 , quando o Brasil ganhou o seu primeiro título e o mundo inteiro era apresentado a Pelé, acompanhar os lances era ou pelo rádio, ou por raras transmissões em preto e branco. A FIFA não vendia patrocínios globais, então as marcas presentes em placas de madeira em volta do campo eram locais, bem contextualizadas mesmo. No fundo da comemoração segundo gol do Brasil, dá pra ver a Telefunken - uma marca alemã de rádios e televisões. Corta para 1994, e o tetra foi transmitido ao vivo e a cores, com a icônica narração de Galvão Bueno. As marcas em volta do campo, por sua vez, já eram conhecidas como Coca-Cola, Gillette, McDonald's e Snickers. Mas o sinal dos tempos aqui é a presença de Fujifilm, Canon, Philips e JVC. O “capturar momentos”, seja em foto, seja em vídeo, estava se popularizando de forma irreversível. Por mais que algumas dessas marcas não estejam mais aqui contando a história… Já em 2002, a Copa do Mundo com sede na Coreia do Sul e Japão marcou a estreia de marcas asiáticas de tecnologia e carros, Toshiba e Hyundai. E o pentacampeonato foi celebrado com outra revolução como plano de fundo - a da internet. (história sendo escrita - não disse qual) Em 2014 nós recebemos o evento em casa e, bom… um baita trauma coletivo também. As placas de LED em volta do campo seguiram intercalando as marcas normalmente conforme o placar ia do zero ao sete sem qualquer piedade. Um dos maiores exemplos de “anti-marketing” de todos os tempos. A ironia, aqui, ficou por conta das marcas alemãs que foram eternizadas nos pesadelos de muita gente - Continental e Adidas. _ Muito se fala sobre o excesso de publicidade ter transformado tudo em paisagem, e de fato não dá para discordar. Uma coisa é ter dez marcas, outra é ter centenas, em diferentes formatos e canais. A Copa de 2026 é uma demonstração inegável disso. Nas últimas semanas, todos os dias teve alguma ação de marca - brindes colecionáveis (de desodorante à delivery), coleções de moda, campanhas publicitárias. Do Ronaldo ao Cafu, até o russo que virou meme em 2018 , está todo mundo virando garoto propaganda. Das transmissões online e conteúdo nas redes sociais aos produtos físicos, se depender das marcas vai ter Copa pra todo lado. (até na pia da cozinha) Mas, apesar da corrida pela atenção ser uma constante para nós, uma ocasião que acontece a cada quatro anos torna tudo um pouco mais ritualístico, mais nostálgico e mais potencialmente histórico. Porque a única certeza que a gente tem nesse mundo acelerado, é que o esporte é o mesmo, mas a próxima Copa do Mundo vai acontecer em um contexto bem diferente dessa. Que já está sendo diferente da anterior. O olhar atento para a Copa do Mundo nos leva das TVs em preto e branco até as criptomoedas. Isso torna as marcas em volta do campo parte de uma narrativa maior. Um espelho do presente - com suas tecnologias, suas questões sociais e, de uns vinte anos para cá, seus memes também. É só olhar em volta. para continuar a conversa nas redes sociais e convidar mais gente para cá, compartilhe usando o botão abaixo ou marcando a @bitstobrands Share para inspirar ✨ Quando a gente fala em “Brasil core” ou em trazer a cultura brasileira para o centro da sua estratégia, essa ação da Cajuína São Geraldo é o melhor exemplo recente. description: nas edições anteriores #296 | O futuro do futuro, pós-SXSW #297 | Escolher o caminho difícil tempo de leitura: 5 minutos para entender 💡 Enquanto profissionais de branding, espera-se que a gente passe a maior parte do tempo no topo do funil - ali nas estratégias para tornar a marca mais conhecida e reconhecida. Mas, nos últimos anos, falamos tanto de brandformance que não é inversão de prioridades questionar como as coisas estão no fundo do funil. Pessoas que são difíceis de segmentar com base em critérios generalistas como demografia ou geração. “O brasileiro passa mais de 9h por dia conectado” não é mais insight. E nem “precisamos estar nas redes sociais porque é lá que as pessoas estão”. Quando abre o celular, o tempo do brasileiro está espalhado por diversos aplicativos que mal aparecem em reuniões de planejamento: um joguinho de Tetris, o app do ônibus, o SofaScore ou até um app de hobby como treino, música ou cinema. E onde tem atenção, tem lembrança, consideração e conversão. _ A Voxus faz mídia programática para diversas marcas no Brasil, com a missão de potencializar conversões. E tem aprendido que isso significa ir em direções totalmente diferentes. Segundo dados da plataforma: Tem rede de academia vendendo em jogos de Tetris. Os aplicativos que mais geram conversões para uma das maiores redes de academia do país são Block Blast e SofaScore. O segundo, a cada 300 impressões gera um usuário para a marca. Parece que o público que treina também confere a tabela do Brasileirão antes de dormir… Tem farmácia convertendo em portais de notícia. O mais comum quando a gente pensa em farmácia talvez seja “aparecer onde as pessoas buscam medicamentos”. Mas os melhores canais de conversão para uma marca do segmento foram UOL, Yahoo e o mesmo Block Blast. Junto, eles somam 22% das conversões. E sneakers premium convertem em apps de ônibus. title: Eight converted power stations that show the power of reuse
description: In this roundup , we take a look at decommissioned power stations that have been given a second life , from the Tate Modern museum in London to the Dyson headquarters in Singapore. Originally built to generate electricity, these industrial buildings typically have expansive interiors with tall ceilings, giving architects plenty of flexibility for conversion. Photo by Hufton & Crow Battersea Power Station, UK, by WilkinsonEyre The Grade II*-listed Battersea Power Station in London stood decommissioned for 39 years before architecture studio WilkinsonEyre 's transformation reopened it as a shopping, office and residential building in 2022. Originally built in the 1930s, a bustling shopping centre is now located in the building's restored turbine halls and glazed apartments were built atop the roof. Find out more about Battersea Power Station › Photo by Peter Sherno Ballers, USA, by Good City Studio and Hexagon Studio Architects Local firms Good City Studio and Hexagon Studio Architects revamped the main turbine hall of Delaware Power Station in Fishtown, Philadelphia , into a sports club with indoor pickleball, soccer and squash courts. Named Ballers, the sports club formed part of the wider plan to transform the 1920s power station into The Battery, a mixed-use complex containing apartments, offices and a hotel. Find out more about Ballers › Photo courtesy of Dyson Dyson headquarters, Singapore, by M Moser Associates, W Architects and Studio Lapis Technology company Dyson established its global company headquarters inside Singapore 's St James Power Station, which was transformed by local studios W Architects and Studio Lapis, with interior fit-out by architecture studio M Moser Associates. The turbine hall of the 1926 building was reimagined as a four-storey atrium framed by exposed black steelwork and a sculptural spiral staircase , while an area of amphitheatre-style seating provides gathering space next to a cafe. Find out more about the Dyson headquarters › Photo by Margherita Spiluttini Tate Modern, UK, by Herzog & de Meuron Iconic London landmark the Tate Modern was once the Bankside Power Station, originally designed by Giles Gilbert Scott, who also designed Battersea Power Station. Swiss studio Herzog & de Meuron 's pioneering transformation of the building opened in 2000, complete with a cathedral-like gallery space in the turbine hall, and ignited a global trend of converting disused power stations into hubs of art and culture. Find out more about Tate Modern › Photo by Iwan Baan Powerhouse Arts, USA, by Herzog & de Meuron In more recent years, Herzog & de Meuron converted the remains of a 115-year-old power plant in Brooklyn into an art manufacturing hub called Powerhouse Arts. The studio refurbished the brick-clad turbine hall, the only part of the original building left standing, and converted it into an art production centre, while the demolished Boiler House was rebuilt in red concrete . Find out more about Powerhouse Arts › Photo by Bai Yu Shajing Village Hall, China, by ARCity Office As part of wider plans to transform an industrial site into a public wetland, architecture studio ARCity Office restored and extended a 1980s power plant in Shenzhen , China, converting it into a community hub . The studio left the building's concrete remnants as-found, using its structural shell to support a series of new steel and glass volumes that draw upon the spaces found in traditional ancestral halls. Find out more about Shajing Village Hall › Photo by Hufton + Crow. Global Leadership Centre, UK, by John McAslan + Partners British studio John McAslan + Partners added learning space and accommodation to Oxford's first electrical power plant to form the Global Leadership Centre, designed for the University of Oxford 's Saïd Business School. John McAslan + Partners created a triple-height entrance and shared space in the turbine hall, restored the 1890s brick facades and rebuilt and extended the metal-clad upper levels. Find out more about Global Leadership Centre › Photo by Tycho Merijn Innovation Powerhouse, the Netherlands, by Atelier van Berlo, Eugelink Architectuur and De Bever Architecten The former Philips power plant in Eindhoven was converted into an innovation hub housing a dozen businesses, with offices arranged along a communal street-like passage. Rotterdam-based Atelier van Berlo worked with Eindhoven-based studios Eugelink Architectuur and De Bever Architecten on the project, aiming to celebrate the building's original features by preserving its structure and coal chutes. title: Objects with Narratives presents collectible design that looks "found rather than fabricated"
description: Belgian gallery Objects with Narratives has curated a texture-heavy exhibition at PAD London called What Remains?, featuring pieces from Ben Storms and Paul Cocksedge . What Remains? marks the second show that Brussels platform Objects with Narratives has presented at design fair PAD London , which takes place annually in Mayfair's Berkley Square. Objects with Narratives has curated a PAD London exhibition called What Remains? The emerging Brussels gallery's exhibition brings together a series of textured pieces united by amorphous shapes and patinated surfaces. "Every piece was crafted in the present, yet many carry a sense of the past, as though found rather than fabricated," said Objects with Narratives. The show features pieces by Ben Storms and Paul Cocksedge Among the exhibitors is Belgian designer Ben Storms , who is known for his rough-hewn furniture that looks like jumbo pillows . Storms is presenting his most recent design, a cushion-like coffee table called Ex Hale, crafted from veiny red Mexican onyx decorated with mosaic veneer. To create the piece, the designer used a hydroforming technique to blow up two pieces of metal sheet that were welded together and 3D-scanned to form a cushion shape. Sofie Middernacht is showing gleaming crimson furniture After this, Storms used a CNC machine to mill the same shape from a block of stone. "Ex Hale plays with our common notions of materiality," said the gallery. "The hard stone looks soft instead, an impression that is further enhanced by the delicate surface treatment." Also on display are Jojo Corväiá's glazed vessels crafted from volcanic clay Also on display is Critical Mass, a handmade Corten steel standing shelf by British designer Paul Cocksedge . A trio of metal components were arranged to support three metal shelves, forming a piece that looks familiar to What Nelson Sees , a weathering steel installation by Cocksedge that was placed in Trafalgar Square for last year's London Design Festival. "The Critical Mass series holds an energy, something on the edge of collapse or explosion," said Objects with Narratives. Read: Armadillo furniture is clad in reused shingles to resemble "friendly monsters" Belgian designer Sofie Middernacht is showing a steel credenza, bench and duo of stools clad in gleaming crimson resin. Middernacht works with discarded industrial materials to create her furniture, which is purposefully formed like archaeological artefacts. Patchwork copper lighting by Karl Monies is included in the show Venezuelan artist Jojo Corväiá is presenting a trio of glazed vessels crafted from volcanic clay, a material central to his practice. A host of other materials feature in the show, from shaggy mohair and wool lamps by Belgian practice KRJST Studio to lighting by Danish designer Karl Monies formed from patchwork slabs of copper. What Remains? runs until 18 October "What Remains? asks what gives an object the sense that it might outlive the moment of its making: the material, the craft, or simply the possibility that some objects belong to no single time at all," Objects with Narratives concluded. Objects with Narratives was founded by Nik and Robbe Vandewyngaerde and Oskar Eryatmaz, who opened their first permanent brick-and-mortar gallery inside a historic 1920s fur atelier in Brussels in 2023. What Remains? is on until 18 October. The photography is by Tijs Vervecken . PAD London 2026 takes place from 14 to 19 October 2026 at Berkeley Square, London W1J 6EN, UK. description: Welcome to the latest edition of OBJECTS QUARTERLY, a roundup of object-related items of interest published, uh, quarterly, for supporters of The Art of Noticing. Attending to objects is a sub-theme of TAoN, and a favorite subject of mine. Revisit prior OQ issues, and other mindful materialism posts, here . Enjoy ! Via Wikipedia . By Arpingstone - Arpingstone, Public Domain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=38786 “KIM’S GAME” Today I have another object-centric attention game borrowed from fiction — borrowed twice over, in fact. It comes from a short story callled “ Kim’s Game, ” by Sadia Shepard, published in The New Yorker earlier this year. In the story, a character recalls a childhood game that his father evidently took from Rudyard Kipling’s Kim : “My father would arrange a handful of objects on a tray—an old coin, a ribbon, a rock, a thimble, that sort of thing—and ask me to memorize them. Then he’d cover the tray with a newspaper and ask me to describe what I remembered. Sometimes, he’d take something away to see if I noticed . In the Kipling novel, the game is part of Kim’s training to be a spy.” This turns out to have become a well-known game , played (with variations) by children, the Cub Scouts , the military, and others. It actually sounds like a fun exercise — and also potentially a great assignment, particularly for a writing class. (And for the record it does sound like decent spy training, too.) If you try it, or have played it in the past, tell me about it! And as always I welcome your object-centered attention games, from fiction or real life. description: * Reminder: The Savor of the Month theme for October is WATER. Details here ; Supporters can share their findings in the thread here . Check it out! Back in August, I tried a little experiment: publishing a question from my ongoing Icebreaker series as a stand-alone post, rather than a secondary item in the main newsletter. The hope was that this would encourage readers to actually answer in the comments. And it did! So I’m doing it again. All are welcome to chime in. Noticing is about other people, too. The Icebreaker series aims to help with that. There’s a central collection spot for all the icebreakers to date, here . Today’s icebreaker comes from me. What is the most recent, or most personally important, book that you’ve read twice (or more)? I would probably stipulate no children’s books; I think that’s a different discussion. But otherwise I’d be open to just seeing where the question leads — I think it’s somehow more interesting than just asking for someone’s “favorite” book. This subject of re-reading books has popped up randomly a couple of times for me lately, and made me think about how long it’s been since I’ve done it. I guess I now worry that I just don’t have enough time to repeat a book when there are so many I haven’t read once! That said, the most recent was The Ladies’ Paradise , by Zola, which I read for a second time about 10 years ago. The book I’ve read the most times is Native Son , three times (all in my 20s, I believe). What about you? Love to hear your thoughts! Leave a comment And please send your favorite icebreaker (whether you made it up or found it elsewhere) to consumed@robwalker.net . Previously: OKAY THAT’S IT! As always, I value your feedback (suggestions, critiques, positive reinforcement, constructive insults directed at me, not at anyone else , etc.), as well as your tips or stories or personal noticing rituals, things we need a word for, and of course your icebreakers : consumed@robwalker.net. Or use the comments. —> Or just click the heart symbol. That always makes my day.
